questions.stem:
The set $T$ represents various traversals over binary tree. The set $S$ represents the order of visiting nodes during a traversal.

Which one of the following is the correct match from $T$ to $S$ ?

rows: L: left subtree, node, right subtree
M: node, left subtree, right subtree
N: left subtree, right subtree, node

options: I – L, II – M, III – N
I – M, II – L, III – N
I – N, II – M, III – L
I – L, II – N, III – M

solutionDiagram.alt: A node with a left and a right subtree, and the three visit orders: inorder is left, node, right (L), preorder is node, left, right (M), postorder is left, right, node (N), with the example tree 1 with children 2 and 3.

steps.title: What a traversal is, and what the three names mean
steps.body: A binary tree is a node that has at most two children, a left child and a right child, and each child is the root of a smaller tree called a subtree. A traversal is a rule for visiting every node exactly once. Every one of the three traversals in the question visits the left subtree before the right subtree. They differ only in when the node itself is visited relative to its two subtrees, and the name says when: pre means before the subtrees, in means between them, post means after them.

steps.title: Read the three orders in the set S
steps.body: Take each row of $S$ and ask where the word node sits. L is left subtree, node, right subtree: the node is between its subtrees. M is node, left subtree, right subtree: the node comes first. N is left subtree, right subtree, node: the node comes last. So L is the inorder rule, M is the preorder rule and N is the postorder rule.

steps.title: Match and check on a small tree
steps.body: I (Inorder) matches L, II (Preorder) matches M, III (Postorder) matches N, which is option A. Check on the tree with root 1 and children 2 (left) and 3 (right): preorder visits 1, 2, 3; inorder visits 2, 1, 3; postorder visits 2, 3, 1. Option B swaps the inorder and preorder rules, option C swaps the inorder and postorder rules, and option D swaps preorder and postorder; none of them reproduces these visit orders.

shortcut.body: Look only at where the word node sits in each S row: middle = inorder, first = preorder, last = postorder. It takes under a minute and never fails, since left always comes before right in all three.

traps.text: Swapping inorder and preorder because both have the node in the same row as the left subtree. Preorder puts the node before the left subtree; inorder puts it after.
Swapping inorder and postorder (I with N, III with L). Inorder has the node in the middle of its subtrees; postorder has it last.
Swapping preorder and postorder: postorder is not node, left, right. Post means after, so the node comes last.

recognize.clues: A table pairs three traversal names with three visiting orders. The cue is the position of the word node relative to the left and right subtrees in each row of S.
recognize.contrast: Not tree reconstruction: no tree is given and nothing is rebuilt. This asks for the definition of each order, whereas reconstruction asks how two orders fix a tree.

check.body: Test the pairing on the tree with root 1, left child 2, right child 3, and 4 as left child of 2. Rule M gives 1, 2, 4, 3; rule L gives 4, 2, 1, 3; rule N gives 4, 2, 3, 1. Only the N order ends at the root and only the M order starts there, so a pairing that gives the root-first rule to a non-pre name fails.

questions.stem:
Consider a binary search tree (BST) with $n$ leaf nodes ($n > 0$). Given any node $V$, the key present in the node is denoted as $\mathrm{Val}(V)$. All the keys present in the given BST are distinct. The keys belong to the set of real numbers.

For a node $V$, let $\mathrm{Suc}(V)$ denote the node that is its inorder successor. If a node $V$ does not have an inorder successor, then $\mathrm{Suc}(V)$ is NULL. As there are no duplicates, if $\mathrm{Suc}(V)$ is not NULL, then $\mathrm{Val}(V) < \mathrm{Val}(\mathrm{Suc}(V))$.

Corresponding to every leaf node $L_i$ that has a non-NULL $\mathrm{Suc}(L_i)$, a new key $k_i$ with the following property is to be inserted into the BST.

$\mathrm{Val}(L_i) < k_i < \mathrm{Val}(\mathrm{Suc}(L_i))$

Let $K$ represent the list of all such new keys to be inserted into the BST.

Which of the following statements is/are true?
options: $K$ will have at least one element
After inserting all keys from $K$, the height of the BST can increase at most by one
Number of nodes in the BST will double after inserting all keys from $K$

solutionDiagram.alt: A BST with leaves 20, 40, 60 and 80. The new keys 25, 45 and 65 sit as dashed right children of 20, 40 and 60; 80 has no successor. The height goes from 2 to 3 and the node count from 7 to 10.

steps.title: The vocabulary and the one rule that decides everything
steps.body: A binary search tree (BST) keeps, at every node, all smaller keys in the left subtree and all larger keys in the right subtree. A leaf is a node with no children. The inorder successor of a node is the node holding the next larger key in the tree. The height is the number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path. To insert a key, start at the root and at each node go left if the key is smaller and right if it is larger; the key becomes a new leaf at the first empty child slot reached. This insertion walk is the single rule: the path taken depends only on how the new key compares with the keys on the way.

steps.title: Where each new key lands
steps.body: Take a leaf $L$ whose successor $S$ exists. $L$ has no right child, so $S$ is the lowest ancestor of $L$ that has $L$ in its left subtree. No key of the tree lies strictly between $\mathrm{Val}(L)$ and $\mathrm{Val}(S)$, because $S$ is the next larger key. Compare the new key $k$ with an ancestor $A$ of $L$. If $\mathrm{Val}(A) < \mathrm{Val}(L)$, then $k$ is larger than $A$ and goes right, as $L$ does. If $\mathrm{Val}(A) > \mathrm{Val}(L)$, then $\mathrm{Val}(A) \ge \mathrm{Val}(S) > k$, so $k$ goes left, as $L$ does. So $k$ follows the path of $L$ exactly, reaches $L$, is larger than it, and becomes the right child of $L$, which was empty. The drawing shows this: dashed nodes 25, 45 and 65 hang to the right of leaves 20, 40 and 60.

steps.title: Statement A: no duplicates
steps.body: Take two leaves with $\mathrm{Val}(L_i) < \mathrm{Val}(L_j)$. The successor of $L_i$ is the next larger key, so $\mathrm{Val}(\mathrm{Suc}(L_i)) \le \mathrm{Val}(L_j)$, and therefore $k_i < \mathrm{Val}(\mathrm{Suc}(L_i)) \le \mathrm{Val}(L_j) < k_j$. The allowed intervals of different leaves never overlap, so the keys of $K$ are all different. A is true.

steps.title: Statement C: height grows by at most one
steps.body: Each $k_i$ is a new leaf directly below its own leaf $L_i$, one level deeper than $L_i$. The old height $h$ is at least the depth of every old leaf, so every new node has depth at most $h+1$, and no new node is placed below another new node because each sits under a different old leaf. The height therefore increases by at most one (by exactly one when a deepest leaf has a successor, as in the example where it goes from 2 to 3). C is true.

steps.title: Statements B and D fail on the smallest trees
steps.body: B says $K$ is never empty. A tree with one node has $n=1$ leaf, the root itself, and that leaf has no successor, so $K$ is empty. A right-leaning chain 1, 2, 3 also has a single leaf, the maximum key, with no successor. B is false. D says the number of nodes doubles. If the tree has $N$ nodes and $n$ leaves, then $|K| \le n$, and doubling needs $|K| = N$. That requires $n = N$, which means every node is a leaf, which happens only for the one-node tree, where $K$ is empty. In the example the count goes from 7 to 10, not 14. D is false. The true statements are A and C.

shortcut.body: Draw a 3-node BST and a 1-node BST. The 1-node tree kills B and D at once (empty $K$, nodes do not double). For A and C use the picture: each new key is the right child of its own leaf, so the new leaves sit one level lower and the intervals between neighbouring keys never overlap. Unsafe step: a single example can refute a statement but not prove it, so trust A and C only because of the insertion argument.

traps.text: Choosing B because in most trees some leaf has a successor. The statement says K will always have an element, and a one-node tree or a right-leaning chain has none.

Choosing D by thinking each leaf produces a child so the tree doubles. Only leaves get a new child, and internal nodes do not, so the count grows by at most the number of leaves, which is less than the node count unless the tree is a single node.
Dropping C by fearing a chain of new keys, one under another. Every new key goes under a different old leaf, so the height rises by one at most.
Dropping A because K is called a list, which could hold repeats. Two different leaves always give disjoint intervals, and one leaf gives one key, so repeats cannot occur.

recognize.clues: New keys are inserted into a BST in the gap between a leaf and its inorder successor. The words inserted into the BST and inorder successor tell you to follow the insertion walk and see where each key lands.
recognize.contrast: Compare bst-deletion, which also uses the inorder successor but to replace a removed node. Here nothing is removed and the successor only marks the upper end of the gap for the new key.

check.body: Boundary case: the BST with root 2, left leaf 1 and right leaf 3. Leaf 1 has successor 2 and leaf 3 has none, so K holds one key between 1 and 2, say 1.5, which becomes the right child of 1. The height goes from 1 to 2 and the nodes from 3 to 4, which is below double. K is non-empty here but the one-node tree makes it empty.

questions.stem:
Let $n$ be an odd number greater than 100. Consider a binary minheap with $n$ elements stored in an array $P$ whose index starts from 1.

Which of the following indices of $P$ do/does NOT correspond to any leaf node of the minheap?

solutionDiagram.alt: A min-heap of 11 nodes drawn as a tree and as an array: positions 1 to 5 are internal (thin), positions 6 to 11 are leaves (thick). Positions 5 and 4 are internal, positions 6 and 11 are leaves.

steps.title: How a heap sits in an array, and what a leaf is
steps.body: A binary heap is a complete binary tree: all levels are full except possibly the last, which fills from the left. It is stored level by level in an array whose index starts at 1, so the root is at index 1. The node at index $i$ has its left child at $2i$ and its right child at $2i+1$, and these children exist only when they are at most $n$. A leaf is a node with no children, so index $i$ is a leaf exactly when $2i > n$. The min-heap ordering (parent smaller than children) does not change positions, so it plays no part here.

steps.title: Split the array into internal nodes and leaves
steps.body: Because $n$ is odd, $n/2$ is a half, and $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor = (n-1)/2$. The indices $1, \dots, (n-1)/2$ satisfy $2i \le n-1$, so each has a left child, and the last of them has children at $n-1$ and $n$. The indices $(n+1)/2, \dots, n$ satisfy $2i \ge n+1 > n$, so they are leaves. The picture for $n=11$ shows internal nodes 1 to 5 and leaves 6 to 11.

steps.title: Test the four options
steps.body: $\frac{n+1}{2}$: here $2i = n+1 > n$, a leaf. $\frac{n-1}{2}$: $2i = n-1 \le n$, so it has children at $n-1$ and $n$, an internal node. $\frac{n-3}{2}$: $2i = n-3 \le n$, internal. $n$: $2n > n$, a leaf. Check with $n=101$: index 51 is a leaf, 50 has children 100 and 101, 49 has children 98 and 99, and 101 is a leaf. The indices that are not leaves are $\frac{n-1}{2}$ and $\frac{n-3}{2}$, options B and C.

shortcut.body: The last internal node is $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor = (n-1)/2$ for odd $n$. Every index up to that value is internal, everything after it is a leaf. So (B) and (C) are at or below the cut and (A), (D) are above it. Plug in $n=11$ to confirm in 30 seconds.

traps.text: Selecting A because $(n+1)/2$ looks like the middle of the array and so like a parent. The cut between internal nodes and leaves is at $(n-1)/2$; the very next index $(n+1)/2$ is already a leaf.
Selecting only B and stopping there, assuming just the last parent is internal. Every index up to $(n-1)/2$ is a parent, so $(n-3)/2$ is also internal and C belongs in the answer.
Selecting D because the last array element feels like a special node. The last element at index $n$ is always a leaf.

recognize.clues: A binary heap with n elements stored in an array from index 1, with indices given as expressions in n. That points to the index arithmetic 2i and 2i+1 for children, not to any key comparison.
recognize.contrast: Not heap-operations: nothing is inserted or deleted and key values never matter. Only positions are asked, unlike bubble-up or heapify questions.

check.body: Count check: the leaves are the indices from the first leaf to n, and the internal nodes are the indices before it. For n = 101 that is 51 leaves and 50 internal nodes, which adds to 101. Also a complete binary tree with an odd node count has no node with a single child, so leaves exceed internal nodes by exactly one: 51 - 50 = 1.

questions.stem: The height of a binary tree is the number of edges in the longest path from the root to a leaf in the tree. The maximum possible height of a full binary tree with 23 nodes is _________. (answer in integer)

solutionDiagram.alt: A tallest full binary tree with 23 nodes: a spine of 11 thick internal nodes, 10 leaves hanging to the left and 2 leaves under the last spine node, down to depth 11.

steps.title: Full binary tree, and the identity that counts its nodes
steps.body: A binary tree is full when every node has either 0 or 2 children. A node with 0 children is a leaf, a node with 2 children is internal. In any tree with $n$ nodes there are $n-1$ edges, since every node except the root has exactly one edge up to its parent. In a full binary tree with $I$ internal nodes each internal node owns 2 edges downward, so the number of edges is $2I$. Setting the two counts equal gives the node count.

steps.title: Count the internal nodes for n = 23
steps.body: $I = (23-1)/2 = 11$ internal nodes and $L = 12$ leaves, which add up to 23.

steps.title: Upper bound on the height
steps.body: Height is the edge count of the longest root-to-leaf path. On a path of $h$ edges, the first $h$ nodes (all but the last) have a child on the path, so they are internal, and the last node is a leaf. Hence $h \le I = 11$.

steps.title: The bound is reached
steps.body: Build a spine of 11 internal nodes, each the child of the one above. Give each of the first 10 spine nodes one extra leaf child, and give the last spine node two leaf children. Every internal node has exactly 2 children, so the tree is full. Nodes: $11 + 10 + 2 = 23$. The root is at depth 0, the last spine node is at depth 10, and its leaves are at depth 11, as in the drawing, so the longest path has 11 edges. The maximum height is 11. A search over every way of splitting 23 nodes between two full subtrees gives the same maximum.

shortcut.body: For a full binary tree, maximum height $=(n-1)/2=11$, because every level on the longest path costs one internal node and a leaf closes the path. Unsafe if the tree is not full: with one-child nodes allowed the maximum is $n-1=22$.

traps.text: Answering 22, the height of a 23-node chain. A chain has nodes with a single child, so it is not full; every node must have 0 or 2 children.
Answering 12 by using the number of leaves (or counting the levels instead of edges). Height counts edges and the longest path has 11 of them.
Answering 10 by forgetting that the last spine node takes two leaves: the extra leaf is what makes the path one edge longer than the spine is tall.
Answering 4, the smallest possible height $\lfloor \log_2 23 \rfloor$. The question asks for the maximum.

recognize.clues: The tree is called full, a node count is given, and the maximum height is asked. The edge-counting identity between nodes, internal nodes and leaves decides how tall the tree can get.
recognize.contrast: Do not use the minimum-height bound of about log base 2 of n, which belongs to complete trees. For a general binary tree with one-child nodes allowed the maximum height would be n - 1, but the full condition rules that out.

check.body: Test the rule on n = 5, where the full shapes can be listed. The only full tree with 5 nodes (up to mirror) is a root with one leaf child and one internal child that has two leaves, and its height is 2, which equals the formula (n - 1)/2. For n = 23 the leaves and internal nodes must also add up: 12 + 11 = 23.

variation.explanation: A full tree with n nodes has (n - 1)/2 internal nodes, here 20. A longest path of h edges uses h internal nodes (every node on it except the last), so h is at most 20. A spine of 20 internal nodes, each with one extra leaf child and the last with two, uses 20 + 19 + 2 = 41 nodes and reaches height 20. This is generated for practice, not an exam question.

questions.stem:
Let $P$ be the set of all integers from 1 to 15. Consider any order of insertion of the elements of $P$ into a binary search tree that creates a complete binary tree.

Which one of the following elements can NEVER be the third element that is inserted?

solutionDiagram.alt: The perfect BST on keys 1 to 15 with root 8. The keys 2, 4, 6, 10, 12 and 14 can be the third key (thick). The key 5 is a leaf under 6 and 4 and needs 8, 4 and 6 first (dashed).

steps.title: Complete tree, BST insertion, and the rule that fixes the order
steps.body: A binary tree is complete when every level is full except possibly the last, which fills from the left. A binary search tree (BST) keeps smaller keys on the left and larger keys on the right. Inserting a key walks down from the root and attaches the key as a new leaf. So the first key inserted is the root, and every later key is attached below keys that are already in the tree. For a fixed final tree the rule is: a node can be inserted only after its parent has been inserted (and then its ancestors too), and any order that respects this rule builds the same tree.
steps.tex: \text{depth}(x)=d\ \Rightarrow\ x \text{ is inserted at position }\ge d+1

steps.title: The final tree is forced
steps.body: A complete binary tree with 15 nodes fills 4 levels exactly (1+2+4+8), so it is the perfect tree of height 3. The inorder of a BST is sorted, so the shape and the keys fix everything: the root has 7 keys on each side, giving 8; its children are 4 and 12; the next level is 2, 6, 10, 14; the leaves are the odd numbers 1, 3, 5, ..., 15.

steps.title: What the third key can be
steps.body: The first key is 8. The second is a child of 8: 4 or 12. If the second is 4, the third can be 12 (child of 8) or 2 or 6 (children of 4). If the second is 12, the third can be 4, or 10, or 14. So the third key is one of 2, 4, 6, 10, 12, 14, as the thick circles show.

steps.title: Check the options
steps.body: 4 is third in the order 8, 12, 4. 2 is third in 8, 4, 2. 10 is third in 8, 12, 10. The key 5 is a child of 6, which is a child of 4, which is a child of 8, so 8, 4 and 6 must all come before it and it is 4th at the earliest. 5 can never be third: option D. An enumeration of all valid prefixes agrees: the possible third keys are 2, 4, 6, 10, 12, 14.

shortcut.body: A node at depth $d$ needs its $d$ ancestors inserted first, so it cannot appear before position $d+1$. The third key has depth at most 2. The odd numbers are the depth-3 leaves, and 5 is the only odd number among the options, so the answer is 5 in under a minute.

traps.text: Excluding 4 because it is on the second level and so looks as if it can only be the second key. If 12 is second, then 4 is a child of 8 that is available third.
Excluding 2 because it is below 4 and so seems to need more keys. It needs only 8 and 4, so 8, 4, 2 is a valid start.
Excluding 10 because it is on the right side, as if the right subtree must wait for the left. The order of the two sides is free, so 8, 12, 10 is valid.

recognize.clues: An insertion order into a BST must produce a complete tree, and the question asks which key can never be third. That links the insertion position of a key to its depth in the fixed final tree.
recognize.contrast: Unlike tree-reconstruction, where given traversals fix the tree, the final tree here is fixed by completeness and the sorted keys, and the question is about which insertion orders build it.

check.body: Try to force 5 into third place. Its ancestors are 8, 4 and 6, three keys, but only two keys come before the third insertion. So 5 cannot be third, however the first two are chosen. The keys 4, 2 and 10 each need at most two ancestors and appear in the orders 8, 12, 4; 8, 4, 2; 8, 12, 10.

questions.stem:
The following sequence corresponds to the preorder traversal of a binary search tree $T$:

$50, 25, 13, 40, 30, 47, 75, 60, 70, 80, 77$

The position of the element 60 in the postorder traversal of $T$ is ______. (answer in integer)

Note: The position begins with 1.

solutionDiagram.alt: The BST rebuilt from the preorder, with the postorder position under every node. 13 is 1, 30 is 2, 47 is 3, 40 is 4, 25 is 5, 70 is 6, 60 is 7, 77 is 8, 80 is 9, 75 is 10 and 50 is 11.

steps.title: Preorder, postorder, and what a BST tells us
steps.body: Preorder visits a node, then its left subtree, then its right subtree. Postorder visits the left subtree, then the right subtree, then the node, so a node comes after everything below it. In a binary search tree (BST) every key in the left subtree is smaller than the node and every key in the right subtree is larger. For a BST, preorder alone rebuilds the tree: the first key is the root, then come all the keys smaller than the root (the left subtree), then all the larger ones (the right subtree).

steps.title: Rebuild the tree
steps.body: Root 50. Smaller keys after it: 25, 13, 40, 30, 47 (left). Larger keys: 75, 60, 70, 80, 77 (right). In the left part, root 25 has the smaller key 13 and the larger keys 40, 30, 47. There, root 40 has smaller 30 and larger 47. In the right part, root 75 has the smaller keys 60, 70 and the larger keys 80, 77. Root 60 has the larger key 70. Root 80 has the smaller key 77. This is the tree in the drawing.

steps.title: Write the postorder and find 60
steps.body: Left subtree of 50 in postorder: 13, 30, 47, 40, 25. Right subtree of 50: its left part 70, 60, then 77, 80, then 75. Root 50 last. The full postorder is 13, 30, 47, 40, 25, 70, 60, 77, 80, 75, 50. Counting from 1, the element 60 is in position 7.

shortcut.body: Do not write the whole postorder. The nodes finished before 60 are the 5 nodes of the left subtree of 50, then 60's own subtree minus 60 itself (the node 70): 5 + 1 = 6 nodes, so 60 is the 7th. Rebuilding the tree is the only real work.

traps.text: Answering 8, which is the position of 60 in the preorder sequence (50, 25, 13, 40, 30, 47, 75, 60). The question asks for the postorder position.
Answering 6 by leaving out 70, which is the right child of 60 and so finishes before 60 in postorder.
Counting from 0, which gives 6; the note says positions begin with 1.

recognize.clues: A BST preorder is given and a postorder position is asked. So rebuild the tree from the preorder using the BST ordering, then read it in postorder.
recognize.contrast: Preorder alone fixes the tree only because it is a BST. For a general binary tree, preorder alone does not determine the tree and a second traversal is needed.

check.body: Second route by counting from the end. The nodes that finish after 60 in postorder are its right sibling's subtree (77, 80), then its parent 75, then the root 50: four nodes. With 11 nodes in all, 60 is at position 11 - 4 = 7.

Preorder lists the root, then the whole left subtree, then the right subtree. In a BST the left keys are smaller than the root and the right keys are larger, so the sequence splits where the keys first exceed the root.

questions.stem:
Consider a binary tree $T$ in which every node has either zero or two children. Let $n > 0$ be the number of nodes in $T$.

Which ONE of the following is the number of nodes in $T$ that have exactly two children?

solutionDiagram.alt: A full binary tree with 7 nodes: the three thick nodes a, b, c have two children each and the four thin nodes d, e, f, g are leaves, so n = 7 gives (n - 1) / 2 = 3 nodes with two children.

steps.title: Edges and children
steps.body: In a tree, every node except the root has exactly one parent, and the link to the parent is one edge. So a tree with $n$ nodes has $n-1$ edges. Counting the same edges from the top, each edge goes from a node down to one of its children, so the number of edges is the sum over all nodes of the number of children of that node.

steps.title: Use the rule that every node has 0 or 2 children
steps.body: Let $t$ be the number of nodes with exactly two children. All other nodes have zero children and add nothing to the sum, so the sum is $2t$. Equating the two counts of edges gives $2t = n-1$.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: For $n=1$ (a lone root) $t=0$. For $n=3$ (root with two leaves) $t=1$. For $n=7$ (the tree in the drawing) $t=3$, and all 429 full binary trees with 15 nodes have $t=7$. The answer is $\frac{n-1}{2}$, option B. The leaves number $n-t=\frac{n+1}{2}$, which is option D, a different quantity.

shortcut.body: Try $n=1$ and $n=3$. With $n=1$ the answer is 0, which only $\frac{n-1}{2}$ gives; with $n=3$ it is 1, which $\frac{n-1}{2}$ also gives. Two tiny trees settle it in under a minute.

traps.text: Choosing A, $\frac{n-2}{2}$, from the idea that the root and one more node are special. With $n=3$ it gives a half.
Choosing C, $\frac{n}{2}$, as 'half the nodes have two children'. That ignores that in a full tree the leaves outnumber the two-child nodes by exactly one.
Choosing D, $\frac{n+1}{2}$. This is the number of leaves, not of nodes with two children.

recognize.clues: Every node has zero or two children, and the count asked is the nodes with exactly two children, in terms of n. This is the edge-counting identity for full binary trees.
recognize.contrast: The number of leaves comes from the same identity but is a different quantity. Read which count the question asks for before choosing a formula.

check.body: Test a case outside the examples: a full tree with 5 nodes, a root with one leaf and one internal child that has two leaves, has 2 nodes with two children, which equals the formula. An even n such as 4 gives a fraction, which shows that no full binary tree has an even number of nodes.

questions.stem:
Suppose the values $10, -4, 15, 30, 20, 5, 60, 19$ are inserted in that order into an initially empty binary search tree. Let $T$ be the resulting binary search tree.

The number of edges in the path from the node containing 19 to the root node of $T$ is ___________. (Answer in integer)

solutionDiagram.alt: The BST after inserting 10, -4, 15, 30, 20, 5, 60 and 19. The thick path from 19 through 20, 30, 15 to the root 10 has four edges.

steps.title: Binary search tree insertion
steps.body: A binary search tree (BST) keeps smaller keys to the left of a node and larger keys to the right. To insert a key, start at the root. At each node go left if the key is smaller and right if it is larger. When the child you need is missing, put the new key there as a leaf. An edge joins a node to its parent, and the path from a node to the root has as many edges as the node has ancestors.
steps.tex: \text{edges from a node to the root}=\text{number of its ancestors}

steps.title: Insert the values one by one
steps.body: 10 becomes the root. -4 is smaller than 10: left of 10. 15 is larger than 10: right of 10. 30 is larger than 10 and 15: right of 15. 20 is larger than 10 and 15, smaller than 30: left of 30. 5 is smaller than 10 and larger than -4: right of -4. 60 is larger than 10, 15 and 30: right of 30. 19 is larger than 10 and 15, smaller than 30 and 20: left of 20.

steps.title: Read off the path
steps.body: The path from 19 goes 19 to 20, 20 to 30, 30 to 15, 15 to 10: four edges. The ancestors of 19 are 20, 30, 15, 10, which are four nodes, matching the thick path in the drawing.

shortcut.body: Only the keys that were on the way to 19 matter. Search for 19 in the tree built so far: it passes 10, 15, 30, 20 (four nodes), so its depth is 4. Do not bother placing 5 or 60, which sit off that path.

traps.text: Answering 5 by counting the nodes on the path, including 19 itself. The question asks for edges, which is one fewer.
Answering 3 by stopping at 30 and making 19 its left child, forgetting that 20 is already there and that 19 < 20 sends 19 one level lower, under 20.
Answering 2 by hanging 19 directly under 15. Since 19 > 15 it goes right, into the subtree of 30, and the comparisons with 30 and 20 push it two levels further down.

recognize.clues: Values are inserted in a stated order into an empty BST and the question asks the path length from one key to the root. That is insertion followed by a depth count.
recognize.contrast: Compare AVL insertion, which rebalances with rotations. Here nothing is rebalanced, so the shape is exactly what the insertion order produces.

check.body: Second route by structure. The key 19 is inserted last, so it is a leaf. In sorted order its neighbours are 15 and 20, and the new leaf must hang off one of them. Node 15 already has the right child 30, so 19 cannot be the right child of 15. Hence 19 is the left child of 20, and 20 sits to the left of 30 (20 < 30) in the right subtree of 15. The path is 10, 15, 30, 20 and then 19, so 19 has four ancestors and four edges to the root.

questions.stem:
A meld operation on two instances of a data structure combines them into one single instance of the same data structure. Consider the following data structures:

P: Unsorted doubly linked list with pointers to the head node and tail node of the list.

Q: Min-heap implemented using an array.

R: Binary Search Tree.

Which ONE of the following options gives the worst-case time complexities for meld operation on instances of size $n$ of these data structures?

solutionDiagram.alt: Three melds: the list needs one pointer from the tail of the first to the head of the second, the array heap is joined into 2n cells and rebuilt with build-heap, and the BST melds by merging the inorder lists and rebuilding a balanced tree. The costs are Theta(1), Theta(n), Theta(n).

steps.title: What meld asks for
steps.body: Meld takes two structures of $n$ elements each and returns one structure with all $2n$ elements that still obeys its own rules. The cost is measured in the worst case and we use the best method for each structure. An unsorted list has no order rule. A min-heap stored in an array is a complete binary tree in which each parent is at most its children. A binary search tree (BST) has smaller keys on the left and larger on the right of every node.

steps.title: P: the linked list costs Theta(1)
steps.body: The list is unsorted, so the order of elements does not matter. With a tail pointer for the first list and a head pointer for the second, make the tail node point to the head node and set the head's back pointer. That is a constant number of pointer changes, independent of $n$.

steps.title: Q: the array heap costs Theta(n)
steps.body: Copy the second array behind the first: $\Theta(n)$. The result is a complete tree but not yet a heap. Run build-heap: sift down every internal node from the middle to the root. Most nodes are near the bottom and move only a step or two, so the total work is linear, not $n \log n$; a count for $n$ from 1000 to 8000 gives about $2.5n$ sift steps for $2n$ elements. The copy already needs $\Omega(n)$ moves, so $\Theta(n)$ is tight.

steps.title: R: the BST costs Theta(n)
steps.body: An inorder walk of each tree produces a sorted list in $\Theta(n)$. Merging two sorted lists takes $\Theta(n)$. Building a balanced BST from a sorted array takes $\Theta(n)$: make the middle element the root and recurse on each half. The three steps add up to $\Theta(n)$ and the output is a valid BST. Inserting the $n$ keys one at a time would cost $\Theta(n\log n)$ in a balanced tree, but it is not the best method. The match is P: $\Theta(1)$, Q: $\Theta(n)$, R: $\Theta(n)$, option A.

shortcut.body: Rule out the options by one value at a time. P is constant with a tail pointer, which removes C. Build-heap is linear, so Q is $\Theta(n)$, which removes B. The balanced rebuild makes R linear, which removes D. What remains is A. Unsafe if the question asked for a heap melded by repeated insertion; then Q would be $n\log n$.

traps.text: Choosing B because inserting the elements of one heap into the other one at a time costs $n \log n$. That is an upper bound for a slow method; build-heap on the joined array does it in linear time.
Choosing C because walking to the end of the list looks like $\Theta(n)$. The tail pointer in the question removes that walk.
Choosing D because BST operations are usually logarithmic, so $n$ inserts look like $n \log n$. Merging the two inorder sequences and rebuilding is linear.

recognize.clues: A meld of three structures where Q is a min-heap stored in an array, P has head and tail pointers, and the question asks for the worst case on size $n$. The array heap is the part that needs a method, not a formula.
recognize.contrast: Not repeated insertion. Inserting the elements of one heap into the other one at a time costs $n\log n$, whereas copying the arrays together and running build-heap once is linear. Tell them apart by asking whether the whole array is rebuilt at once.

check.body: Two-sided check on Q. Lower bound: the meld must read all $2n$ elements, so Q is $\Omega(n)$. Upper bound: build-heap costs at most the sum over heights $h$ of (nodes at height $h$) times $h$, and a heap of $m$ nodes has at most $\lceil m/2^{h+1}\rceil$ nodes at height $h$, so the sum is at most about $m\sum_h h/2^{h+1}=m$. With $m=2n$ that is $O(n)$, so $\Theta(n\log n)$ for Q is too large. The same size argument gives the lower bound for R, and the list needs no reads, so a constant is possible there.

questions.stem: Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE for any binary search tree (BST) having $n$ distinct integers?
options: The maximum length of a path from the root node to any other node is $(n-1)$.
An inorder traversal will always produce a sorted sequence of elements.
Finding an element takes $O(\log_2 n)$ time in the worst case.
Every BST is also a Min-Heap.

solutionDiagram.alt: Left: a BST built from 1, 2, 3, 4 in order is a chain with longest path n - 1 = 3 edges and a search for 4 takes 4 comparisons. Right: the tree 2 with children 1 and 3 has sorted inorder 1 2 3 but is not a min-heap.

steps.title: Four terms and the rule behind them
steps.body: A binary search tree (BST) has, at every node, smaller keys on its left and larger keys on its right. A path from the root counts its edges; its length is the number of edges. Inorder traversal visits left subtree, node, right subtree. A min-heap is a complete binary tree where every parent is at most its children. The worst case of a statement 'for any BST' means a plain BST with no balancing rule, so the shape depends on the insertion order and can be a chain.

steps.title: A is true: path length is at most n - 1
steps.body: A path from the root visits distinct nodes, so a path can contain at most $n$ nodes and therefore $n-1$ edges. A BST that was built by inserting sorted keys is a chain and reaches this bound. The statement is read as the largest value the length can take, and the key accepts it. In the drawing the chain 1, 2, 3, 4 has a longest path of 3 edges.

steps.title: B is true: inorder is sorted
steps.body: By induction on the number of nodes. The inorder of a tree is the inorder of the left subtree, then the node, then the inorder of the right subtree. By hypothesis each part is sorted, every left key is smaller than the node, and every right key is larger. The concatenation is sorted.

steps.title: C and D are false
steps.body: C: a plain BST built from sorted keys is a chain, and finding the largest key then costs $n$ comparisons, which is $\Theta(n)$ and not $O(\log_2 n)$. Only balanced trees such as AVL give $O(\log n)$. D: the BST with root 2 and children 1 and 3 is not a min-heap, since the root 2 is larger than its child 1. In general a BST puts the smaller key on the left, which is below the parent. The true statements are A and B.

shortcut.body: Test C and D with tiny trees: a chain 1, 2, 3, 4 kills C, and the tree 2(1, 3) kills D. B is the definition of a BST. A is the upper bound on path length. About a minute for the whole question.

traps.text: Marking C as true because textbooks say BST search is $O(\log n)$. That is for balanced BSTs; a plain BST can be a chain.
Marking D as true by mixing up BST order with heap order. A BST orders left, node, right; a heap orders parent against child.
Leaving out A because a balanced BST has paths much shorter than $n-1$. The statement is the worst-case bound over all BSTs, and the key counts it as true.
Leaving out B. Inorder gives a sorted list for every BST with distinct keys, and not only for balanced ones.

recognize.clues: The words "any BST" and "worst case", with four statements about path length, inorder order, search time and heap order. Each needs a shape that is allowed but not balanced.
recognize.contrast: A plain BST against a balanced tree such as AVL: only the balanced tree has $O(\log n)$ search. A BST against a min-heap: the BST compares left, node and right across whole subtrees, while a heap compares only a parent with its children.

check.body: Enumerate all 24 insertion orders of 4 keys. The longest root path reaches 3 edges for the sorted orders, the inorder is 1, 2, 3, 4 for every order, and finding the key 4 costs 4 comparisons for the ascending order. No order gives a min-heap, because a heap with 4 nodes has a left child at the root and a BST puts a smaller key there.

variation.stem: Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE for any binary search tree having $n \ge 2$ distinct integers?
options: The smallest key is reached from the root by following left child pointers only.
A preorder traversal always produces a sorted sequence.
The root always holds the median key.
The height of the tree, counted in edges, is at least $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$.
variation.explanation: Smaller keys go left, so the minimum is the end of the left chain. A tree with $n$ nodes and at most two children per node needs at least $\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor$ levels below the root, so the height bound holds. Preorder starts at the root, which is not the smallest key in general, and the root is whichever key was inserted first, not the median.

questions.stem:
The height of any rooted tree is defined as the maximum number of edges in the path from the root node to any leaf node.

Suppose a Min-Heap $T$ stores 32 keys. The height of $T$ is _____________. (Answer in integer)

solutionDiagram.alt: The levels of a heap with 32 keys: level 0 holds 1 node, level 1 holds 2, level 2 holds 4, level 3 holds 8, level 4 holds 16, and level 5 holds the single node 32. The height is 5.

steps.title: What a heap looks like and how its height is counted
steps.body: A binary min-heap is a complete binary tree: every level is full except possibly the last, which fills from the left. Level $k$ (the root is level 0) holds up to $2^k$ nodes. The height is the number of edges from the root to the deepest leaf, which equals the index of the deepest level. The min-heap ordering does not change this shape, so the height depends only on the number of keys $n$.

steps.title: Fill the levels
steps.body: Levels 0 to 4 hold $1+2+4+8+16 = 31$ nodes when full. A heap with 32 keys has those 31 nodes plus one more, which starts level 5 at its leftmost position (array index 32). So the deepest level is level 5.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: The height equals $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$. Here $\log_2 32 = 5$ exactly, so the height is 5.

shortcut.body: Height of a heap with $n$ keys is $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$. Since $32 = 2^5$, the answer is 5 straight away. For $n=31$ the same formula gives 4, the case of a perfect tree.

traps.text: Answering 6 by counting levels (there are 6 levels, 0 to 5) rather than edges, or by using $\lceil \log_2(n+1)\rceil = \lceil \log_2 33\rceil$. The definition in the question counts edges.
Answering 4 because a perfect tree of height 4 has 31 nodes. With 32 keys one more node spills onto a new level.
Answering 16 or 32 by confusing the height with the number of leaves or keys.

recognize.clues: A min-heap with 32 keys and a definition of height counted in edges. The number of keys alone fixes the shape.
recognize.contrast: Height counted in edges against levels counted in nodes differ by one. And 32 is a power of two, the boundary where a perfect tree would hold 31 or 63 keys, so a formula applied loosely is easy to be off by one.

check.body: Boundary check: a heap with 31 keys is a perfect tree of height 4, so adding the 32nd key must raise the height by one at exactly this size. Second route: the last key sits at array index 32, and halving the index to reach the parent each time goes 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, which is 5 steps, one per edge up to the root.

questions.stem:
You are given a set $V$ of distinct integers. A binary search tree $T$ is created by inserting all elements of $V$ one by one, starting with an empty tree. The tree $T$ follows the convention that, at each node, all values stored in the left subtree of the node are smaller than the value stored at the node. You are not aware of the sequence in which these values were inserted into $T$, and you do not have access to $T$.

Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: Inorder traversal of $T$ can be determined from $V$
Root node of $T$ can be determined from $V$
Preorder traversal of $T$ can be determined from $V$
Postorder traversal of $T$ can be determined from $V$

solutionDiagram.alt: Two BSTs on the set {1, 2, 3}. Inserting 2, 1, 3 gives preorder 2 1 3, inorder 1 2 3 and postorder 1 3 2. Inserting 1, 2, 3 gives preorder 1 2 3, inorder 1 2 3 and postorder 3 2 1. Only the inorder is the same.

steps.title: What is fixed by the set, and what by the order
steps.body: A binary search tree (BST) keeps smaller keys in the left subtree and larger keys in the right subtree. Inserting a key walks down from the root and attaches it as a leaf, so the first key inserted becomes the root, and the shape of the tree depends on the insertion order. The set $V$ is only the collection of keys; it says nothing about the order. The question is therefore which traversal comes out the same for every insertion order of $V$. The three traversals are inorder (left, node, right), preorder (node, left, right) and postorder (left, right, node).

steps.title: Inorder is always the sorted V
steps.body: In the inorder sequence every node appears after all keys of its left subtree and before all keys of its right subtree. By the BST property that is exactly the sorted order of those keys. By induction on the size, the inorder of any BST on $V$ is $V$ in increasing order, whatever order the keys were inserted in. So inorder is determined by $V$.

steps.title: The others change with the order
steps.body: Take $V=\{1,2,3\}$. Inserting 2, 1, 3 gives root 2 with children 1 and 3: preorder 2, 1, 3 and postorder 1, 3, 2. Inserting 1, 2, 3 gives a chain with root 1: preorder 1, 2, 3 and postorder 3, 2, 1. The root, the preorder and the postorder all differ while the inorder stays 1, 2, 3. For $V=\{1,2,3,4\}$ all 24 insertion orders give 4 different roots, 14 different preorders and 14 different postorders, but a single inorder. The answer is A.

shortcut.body: Ask which of the four does not depend on insertion order. The root is the first inserted key, preorder and postorder follow the shape, and only inorder is the sorted list. One 3-key example (2, 1, 3 against 1, 2, 3) confirms it.

traps.text: Choosing B because the root of a BST is often imagined as the median. Any key can be the root; it is the first key inserted.
Choosing C: preorder starts at the root, which is not fixed, and then follows the shape, so it changes with the insertion order.
Choosing D for the same reason as C. Postorder ends with the root and also depends on the shape.

recognize.clues: Only the set $V$ is known and the insertion order is hidden. The question asks which traversal or property is determined by the set.
recognize.contrast: Not tree reconstruction (pds-trees.tree-reconstruction): reconstruction needs inorder together with another traversal to fix one tree. Here the set fixes the inorder sequence alone, and does not fix the tree.

check.body: Count by enumeration. For the 3 keys 1, 2, 3 there are 6 insertion orders, which give 5 distinct trees. Across them there are 3 different roots, 5 different preorders, 5 different postorders and exactly 1 inorder sequence. A property that takes one value over every order is the one the set determines.

questions.stem: An array $[82, 101, 90, 11, 111, 75, 33, 131, 44, 93]$ is heapified. Which one of the following options represents the first three elements in the heapified array?

solutionDiagram.alt: Left: the array 82, 101, 90, 11, 111, 75, 33, 131, 44, 93 as a tree. Right: the max-heap after build-heap, 131, 111, 90, 101, 93, 75, 33, 11, 44, 82, with the first three elements in thick circles.

steps.title: Heap, heapify, sift-down
steps.body: A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array with index starting at 1: the children of position $i$ are $2i$ and $2i+1$. In a max-heap each parent is at least as large as its children, so the maximum sits at position 1. To heapify (build-heap) an array, process the internal nodes from the last one, position $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, down to position 1. For each, sift down: while the node is smaller than its larger child, swap them. Of the four options only a max-heap can match, since two of them start with the maximum 131 and the other two with 82, which is neither the maximum nor the minimum of the array.

steps.title: Sift down positions 5 to 3
steps.body: Array positions 1 to 10: 82, 101, 90, 11, 111, 75, 33, 131, 44, 93. Position 5 holds 111, its child at 10 is 93: no swap. Position 4 holds 11, its children are 131 and 44: swap 11 with 131, giving 82, 101, 90, 131, 111, 75, 33, 11, 44, 93 (11 now at position 8 with no children). Position 3 holds 90, its children are 75 and 33: no swap.

steps.title: Sift down positions 2 and 1
steps.body: Position 2 holds 101, its children are 131 and 111: swap with 131, giving 82, 131, 90, 101, 111, 75, 33, 11, 44, 93 (101 at position 4 has children 11 and 44, so it stays). Position 1 holds 82, its children are 131 and 90: swap with 131, giving 131, 82, 90, 101, 111, ... Then 82 at position 2 has children 101 and 111: swap with 111, giving 131, 111, 90, 101, 82, ... Then 82 at position 5 has child 93 at position 10: swap, giving the final array.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: The heapified array is 131, 111, 90, 101, 93, 75, 33, 11, 44, 82, and its first three elements are 131, 111, 90: option D. Inserting the keys one at a time into an empty max-heap gives the same first three elements. Reading 'heapified' as a min-heap would give 11, 44, 33, which is not offered.

shortcut.body: The root of a max-heap is the array maximum, 131, which removes A and B. Position 2 must be the largest of the subtree below it, so it cannot be 11, the smallest key of the whole array. That removes C and leaves D. Unsafe if the question wanted a min-heap, but no option starts with 11.

traps.text: Choosing A, 82, 90, 101: the root 82 is neither the maximum nor the minimum, so no heap can start with it; it is nearly the unchanged input.
Choosing B, 82, 11, 93: it also keeps 82 at the root, and 11 above bigger keys breaks the heap rule.
Choosing C: the root 131 is right, but 11 at position 2 would have bigger children (101 or 111) below it. Sift-down moves 11 to a leaf.

recognize.clues: An array being heapified, and the question asks for the first three elements of the result. The word heapified points at build-heap.
recognize.contrast: Build-heap against inserting the keys one at a time: they can give different arrays, so the order of work matters. Also max-heap against min-heap: the options settle which one is meant, since the root must be the extreme key.

check.body: Two independent tests on the final array 131, 111, 90, 101, 93, 75, 33, 11, 44, 82. First, it is a rearrangement of the input: the keys add up to 771 in both. Second, every position $j\ge2$ holds a key no larger than the one at position $\lfloor j/2\rfloor$, for example 93 under 111 and 82 under 93.

questions.stem: Consider a binary min-heap containing 105 distinct elements. Let $k$ be the index (in the underlying array) of the maximum element stored in the heap. The number of possible values of $k$ is

solutionDiagram.alt: The array of a min-heap with 105 elements: positions 1 to 52 are internal nodes and positions 53 to 105 are the 53 leaves. The maximum must sit on a leaf, so k has 53 possible values.

steps.title: Min-heap in an array
steps.body: A binary min-heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array, with the root at index 1 and the children of index $i$ at $2i$ and $2i+1$. The rule is that every parent is smaller than each of its children. A leaf is an index $i$ with $2i > n$, because its left child would be past the end. An internal node has at least one child that is larger than it.

steps.title: The maximum must be a leaf
steps.body: If a node had a child, that child would be larger, so the node could not be the maximum. Hence the maximum sits on a leaf. Internal nodes are the indices with $2i \le 105$, that is $i \le 52$. Leaves are $53, 54, \dots, 105$, which is $105-52 = 53$ positions.

steps.title: Every leaf is possible
steps.body: For a leaf index $k$, put the largest value at $k$ and fill the other 104 positions with the smaller values in increasing order along the array. A parent has a smaller index than its child, so it gets a smaller value, and the maximum at $k$ has no children. This is a valid min-heap with the maximum at $k$. A direct check over all 105 positions finds exactly the 53 positions 53 to 105. The number of possible values of $k$ is 53, option A.

shortcut.body: Count the leaves of a heap with $n$ nodes: $n-\lfloor n/2\rfloor = 105-52 = 53$. The maximum of a min-heap always sits on a leaf and any leaf can hold it, so the answer is the leaf count.

traps.text: Choosing 52, which is the number of internal nodes, $\lfloor 105/2\rfloor$. The maximum is on a leaf, not on an internal node.
Choosing 27 by counting only some leaves, for example those under one child of the root. The maximum can be on any leaf.
Choosing 1 by assuming the maximum is always in the last position, as in a sorted array. A heap is only partly ordered, so any leaf can hold it.

recognize.clues: A min-heap of 105 distinct elements, and the question asks how many array indices can hold the maximum.
recognize.contrast: The maximum of a min-heap (any leaf, many indices) against the minimum (always the root, one index). The two look alike but have different counts.

check.body: Small cases by brute force over every permutation that forms a min-heap: for $n=5, 6, 7$ the maximum occupies 3, 3 and 4 different positions, and each count equals $n-\lfloor n/2\rfloor$. The same formula for $n=105$ gives the answer.

questions.stem: Which one of the following sequences when stored in an array at locations $A[1], \ldots, A[10]$ forms a max-heap?

solutionDiagram.alt: Four candidate arrays drawn as heaps of 10 nodes: A breaks the max-heap rule at 14 under 10 and at 7 under 6, B satisfies it everywhere, C breaks it at 7 under 6 and at 15 under 13, D breaks it at 12 and 7 under 1

steps.title: What a max-heap in an array is, and the one test that decides it
steps.body: A binary heap is a complete binary tree: every level is full except possibly the last, which fills from the left. It is stored level by level in an array, so the root is $A[1]$, and the node at index $j$ has its parent at index $\lfloor j/2 \rfloor$. In a max-heap every parent is at least as large as each of its children. That parent-child rule is the whole test: a sequence is a max-heap exactly when no child is larger than its parent. Nothing is required between siblings or between cousins.

steps.title: Which pairs to compare
steps.body: With 10 elements the children are the indices 2 to 10, so there are 9 parent-child pairs. The parents of indices 2 and 3 are index 1; of 4 and 5, index 2; of 6 and 7, index 3; of 8 and 9, index 4; of 10, index 5. The drawing places each option in a tree with this numbering and marks the pairs that break the rule.

steps.title: Options A, C and D each break the rule
steps.body: Option A: $A[6]=14$ sits under its parent $A[3]=10$, and $14 > 10$. Also $A[9]=7$ sits under $A[4]=6$. Option C: $A[9]=7$ sits under $A[4]=6$, and $A[10]=15$ sits under $A[5]=13$. Option D: $A[8]=12$ and $A[9]=7$ both sit under $A[4]=1$. A single violation is enough to rule an option out.

steps.title: Option B passes every pair
steps.body: The nine pairs of option B (23, 17, 14, 7, 13, 10, 1, 5, 6, 12) are: $17 \le 23$, $14 \le 23$, $7 \le 17$, $13 \le 17$, $10 \le 14$, $1 \le 14$, $5 \le 7$, $6 \le 7$, $12 \le 13$. All hold, so B is a max-heap. The answer is option B.

shortcut.body: Start at the bottom, where mistakes hide: compare $A[9]$ with $A[4]$ and $A[10]$ with $A[5]$. Option A fails at $A[9]=7 > A[4]=6$, option C fails at the same pair, and option D fails because $A[4]=1$ has bigger children. Only B is left, so check nothing else. This is unsafe if you stop after looking only at the root and its children, because all four options pass that check.

traps.text: Choosing A because 23 is the largest and sits at the root, and 17 and 10 look fine. The root being the maximum is necessary, not sufficient: 14 at index 6 is bigger than its parent 10 at index 3.
Choosing C because the last number 15 looks like a big value in a safe place. Its parent is $A[5]=13$, and $15 > 13$, so the rule fails; also $7 > 6$ at indices 9 and 4.
Choosing D because the first two levels look right (14 and 17 are both below 23). The rule must hold at every level: index 4 holds 1, yet its children 12 and 7 are larger.

recognize.clues: Four sequences stored at $A[1]$ to $A[10]$, and the question asks which forms a max-heap. All four start with the largest key, so the root alone does not decide it.
recognize.contrast: A max-heap against a binary search tree: a BST needs left, node, right order across whole subtrees, while a heap compares only a parent with its children and ignores the order of siblings.

check.body: A second route is to run the sift-down pass of build-heap on each option. On a valid max-heap it makes no swap at all; on an invalid one it swaps at least once. Running it on the four options changes three of them and leaves exactly one unchanged.

questions.stem:
Let $A$ be a priority queue for maintaining a set of elements. Suppose $A$ is implemented using a max-heap data structure. The operation Extract-Max($A$) extracts and deletes the maximum element from $A$. The operation Insert($A$,key) inserts a new element key in $A$. The properties of a max-heap are preserved at the end of each of these operations.

When $A$ contains $n$ elements, which one of the following statements about the worst case running time of these two operations is TRUE?
options: Both Extract-Max($A$) and Insert($A$,key) run in $O(1)$.
Both Extract-Max($A$) and Insert($A$,key) run in $O(\log(n))$.
Extract-Max($A$) runs in $O(1)$ whereas Insert($A$,key) runs in $O(n)$.
Extract-Max($A$) runs in $O(1)$ whereas Insert($A$,key) runs in $O(\log(n))$.

solutionDiagram.alt: Left: inserting into a max-heap of 15 nodes puts the new key in slot 16 and sifts it up along the path 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, at most 4 swaps; right: Extract-Max moves the last key to the root and sifts it down along one root-to-leaf path of at most 3 swaps; both are paths of length at most the height, floor(log2 n)

steps.title: Priority queue, max-heap, and what worst case means here
steps.body: A priority queue holds elements and always hands back the one with the largest key. A max-heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array in which every parent is at least as large as its children, so the maximum sits at the root. A complete tree with $n$ nodes has height $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$, because each level holds twice as many nodes as the one above. Worst-case running time is the largest number of steps over all inputs of size $n$. Both operations must leave the heap valid, and repairing it means moving one key along one root-to-leaf path.
steps.tex: \text{height of a complete tree with } n \text{ nodes} = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor

steps.title: Insert: sift up
steps.body: Put the new key in the first free slot, which is the end of the array and costs $O(1)$. Its parent may now be smaller, so while the key is larger than its parent, swap them. Each swap moves the key one level up, so there are at most as many swaps as the height. In the drawing, a heap of 15 keys receives the key in slot 16, and the path 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 allows at most 4 swaps. Insert is $O(\log n)$.

steps.title: Extract-Max: sift down
steps.body: Reading the maximum at the root is $O(1)$, but extracting it removes the root and leaves a hole. Fill it with the last key of the array and shrink the heap by one. That key is usually small, so while it is smaller than a child, swap it with the larger child. Each swap moves it one level down, so there are at most $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ swaps. In the worst case the key falls all the way to a leaf, so Extract-Max is $\Theta(\log n)$, not $O(1)$.

steps.title: Match the options
steps.body: Both operations are $O(\log n)$, which is option B. Option A is false because neither operation is constant. Option C is false because Extract-Max is not $O(1)$ (and the $O(n)$ bound on Insert is true but far looser than the real cost). Option D is false because Extract-Max is not $O(1)$ in the worst case. Random heaps of sizes 15, 255 and 1023 confirm that the worst number of swaps grows with the height for both operations.

shortcut.body: Both operations walk one path in a tree whose height is $\log n$. Only B says $O(\log n)$ for both. Unsafe step: Find-Max alone is $O(1)$; the question asks about Extract-Max, which includes the repair.

traps.text: Choosing A because the maximum is at the root. That makes reading it constant, but removing it leaves a gap that costs a sift down, and Insert also needs a sift up.
Choosing C: Insert is $O(n)$ is a true statement only as a loose bound, and Extract-Max $O(1)$ is false because the heap must be repaired after the root is removed.
Choosing D because Insert looks logarithmic and the maximum looks free. Taking the root out destroys the shape of the heap, and restoring it takes up to $\log n$ swaps.

recognize.clues: A priority queue held as a max-heap, with the worst-case running time asked for both Insert and Extract-Max.
recognize.contrast: Find-Max, which only reads the root in constant time, against Extract-Max, which also repairs the heap. And building a heap from $n$ keys at once (linear) against inserting them one by one ($n\log n$).

check.body: Simulate on heaps of $2^k-1$ keys, built in descending order so that the repair runs the full length. Inserting a new largest key makes $k$ swaps and extracting the maximum makes $k-1$ swaps, for $k$ from 3 to 10 (7 up to 1023 keys). The count rises by one each time the size doubles, which is logarithmic growth, neither constant nor linear.

questions.stem:
Consider the C function foo and the binary tree shown.

When foo is called with a pointer to the root node of the given binary tree, what will it print?
questions.figure: A binary tree with 6 nodes. The root holds 10. Its left child holds 5 and its right child holds 11. Node 5 has a left child 3 and a right child 8, and both are leaves. Node 11 has no left child and a right child 13, which is a leaf.

diagram.alt: Binary tree for the C function foo: root 10 with left child 5 and right child 11; 5 has children 3 and 8; 11 has right child 13

solutionDiagram.alt: The same tree with the value foo returns at each node and the order of the printf calls: 3 prints first, then 8, 16, 13, 24 and 50

steps.title: What the function computes, and where it prints
steps.body: A binary tree node holds a value and two pointers, left and right, and a pointer can be NULL, meaning no child. foo is recursive: for a node p it calls itself on the left child, then on the right child, and only then runs the printf. So a node prints after both of its subtrees have finished, which is the postorder rule (left, right, node). What it prints is not the key but retval, which is the key plus the two values returned by the children, and a NULL child returns 0. By induction, foo(p) returns the sum of all keys in the subtree rooted at p.

steps.title: The left subtree of the root
steps.body: Node 3 is a leaf: it returns $3 + 0 + 0 = 3$ and prints 3. Node 8 is a leaf and prints 8. Then node 5, whose two subtrees are done, computes $5 + 3 + 8 = 16$ and prints 16. The left side has printed 3, 8, 16.

steps.title: The right subtree of the root
steps.body: Node 11 calls foo on its left, which is NULL and returns 0 without printing, then on its right child 13. Node 13 is a leaf and prints 13. Then node 11 computes $11 + 0 + 13 = 24$ and prints 24. The right side has printed 13, 24.

steps.title: The root and the answer
steps.body: After both subtrees are finished, the root computes $10 + 16 + 24 = 50$ and prints 50. The full output is 3 8 16 13 24 50, which is option C. The drawing writes the value returned at each node and numbers the prints from first to last.

shortcut.body: The last printed number is the sum of all keys, $3+5+8+10+11+13 = 50$, and the first is the leftmost leaf, 3. Only C ends in 50, so the answer is C. As a check, D prints 16 before 8, which cannot happen because node 5 prints only after its child 8 is done.

traps.text: Choosing A: this is the plain postorder of the keys. The function prints retval, the subtree sum, not the key.
Choosing B: this is the sorted order (inorder) of the keys. The printf runs after both recursive calls, not between them, and it prints sums.
Choosing D: sums are right but the order is inorder (3, 5, 8, 10, 11, 13 with sums 3, 16, 8, 50, 24, 13). The printf is after both calls, so a parent prints after both children.

questions.stem: Suppose a binary search tree with 1000 distinct elements is also a complete binary tree. The tree is stored using the array representation of binary heap trees. Assuming that the array indices start with 0, the 3rd largest element of the tree is stored at index_____________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Complete binary tree with 1000 nodes in a 0-indexed array: the right spine is 0, 2, 6, 14, 30, 62, 126, 254, 510 and node 510 is the largest key; its parent 254 is next; the last node before 254 in inorder is 509, the rightmost node of the left subtree of 254, so the third largest is at index 509

steps.title: The words in the question, and the two rules that decide it
steps.body: A binary search tree (BST) keeps smaller keys in the left subtree and larger keys in the right subtree, so reading its nodes in inorder (left, node, right) gives the keys in increasing order. A complete binary tree has every level full except possibly the last, which fills from the left. In the array representation with indices from 0, the node at index $i$ has its left child at $2i+1$ and its right child at $2i+2$, and a child exists only if its index is at most $n-1 = 999$. The 3rd largest key is the 3rd node from the end of the inorder sequence, and the node just before a node $x$ in inorder is the largest key of the left subtree of $x$ if $x$ has one, otherwise the nearest ancestor that has $x$ in its right subtree.

steps.title: The largest key
steps.body: The largest key is the last node of inorder, reached by going right from the root until there is no right child. The right children are 2, then 6, 14, 30, 62, 126, 254, 510. The next right child would be $2 \cdot 510 + 2 = 1022 > 999$, so the walk stops. The largest key is at index 510.

steps.title: The 2nd largest key
steps.body: Node 510 has no left child, since $2 \cdot 510 + 1 = 1021 > 999$. With no left subtree, the node before it in inorder is the nearest ancestor of which it is in the right subtree. Its parent 254 has 510 as its right child. So the 2nd largest key is at index 254.

steps.title: The 3rd largest key
steps.body: Node 254 has a left child at $2 \cdot 254 + 1 = 509$, which exists, so the node before 254 in inorder is the largest key of that left subtree. Start at 509 and go right: $2 \cdot 509 + 2 = 1020 > 999$, so 509 has no right child and is itself the largest key of its subtree. The 3rd largest key is at index 509. Check with the sizes: levels 0 to 8 are full and hold $2^9 - 1 = 511$ nodes (indices 0 to 510), and the remaining 489 nodes sit in level 9 starting from index 511, so 509 and 510 are leaves.

shortcut.body: Levels 0 to 8 are full ($511$ nodes), so the last full level ends at index 510, and 510 is the largest key. The second largest is its parent $(510-2)/2 = 254$, and the third largest is the left child of that parent, $2 \cdot 254 + 1 = 509$. Unsafe when the last level reaches the right edge: then the left child of 254 would have a left subtree of its own, and you would have to go further right inside it.

traps.text: Answering 510: that is the index of the largest key (the end of the right spine), or the position of the 3rd largest key if the array were numbered from 1.
Answering 254: that is the 2nd largest key, the parent of the largest. The 3rd largest is the key just before it in inorder.
Answering 999 or 998: the last array entries are the bottom-level leaves read left to right, not the largest keys. The array is in level order, not sorted order.

recognize.clues: The tree is stored in an array with indices from 0, so child positions follow $2i+1$ and $2i+2$. The question asks for the index of the 3rd largest key of a BST that is also complete, which links array positions to inorder positions.
recognize.contrast: Not a heap-order question: nothing says the tree is a heap, so the maximum is not at index 0. The BST property puts the largest key at the end of the right spine.

check.body: Count the nodes below the claimed positions. Levels 0 to 8 are full and use indices 0 to 510, so the last full level ends at 510. Every index from 511 to 999 is a bottom-level leaf. Cross-check by listing the inorder end: a script that runs inorder on the 1000-node array tree ends with the indices of the three largest keys, and the third from the end is the one found by walking the spine.

questions.stem: Let $H$ be a binary min-heap consisting of $n$ elements implemented as an array. What is the worst case time complexity of an optimal algorithm to find the maximum element in $H$?

solutionDiagram.alt: Binary min-heap of 15 values in array positions 1 to 15: every parent is smaller than its children, so the maximum 15 is at a leaf; positions 8 to 15 are the 8 leaves (thick), and any leaf could hold the maximum

steps.title: What a min-heap promises, and what it does not
steps.body: A binary min-heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array in which every parent is smaller than or equal to its children. So the smallest key is at the root and a key is never smaller than its parent. A leaf is a node with no children. In the array of $n$ elements, the node at index $i$ is a leaf when $2i > n$, so the leaves are the last $\lceil n/2 \rceil$ positions. The order rule only relates a parent to its own children. It says nothing about two nodes that are not on one root-to-leaf path, and in particular nothing about two leaves.

steps.title: Where the maximum can be
steps.body: An internal node has a child that is at least as large as itself, so an internal node holds the maximum value only if a leaf below it holds the same value. So some leaf always holds the maximum. The drawing shows a heap of 15 keys: the 8 leaves (thick) hold 15, 9, 8, 11, 12, 14, 10, 13, and the maximum 15 sits at the first leaf, but with another input it could sit at any of them.

steps.title: Why every leaf must be looked at
steps.body: Suppose an algorithm skips one leaf $x$. Replace $x$ by a value larger than everything else. The heap rule still holds, because $x$ has no children and its parent only has to be smaller than it. The algorithm never saw the change, so it gives the same answer, which is now wrong. Hence every one of the $\lceil n/2 \rceil$ leaves must be read, so $\Omega(n)$ is needed.

steps.title: The upper bound and the answer
steps.body: Scanning the whole array once finds the maximum with $n-1$ comparisons, so $O(n)$ is enough. Together with the lower bound the cost is $\Theta(n)$, which is option C.

shortcut.body: The maximum of a min-heap is hidden among about $n/2$ leaves that are not ordered against each other, so there is no shortcut over reading them: $\Theta(n)$. Unsafe if you confuse it with a max-heap (maximum at the root, $\Theta(1)$) or with Delete-Min ($\Theta(\log n)$).

traps.text: Choosing $\Theta(1)$: the root of a min-heap holds the minimum, not the maximum. $\Theta(1)$ would be correct for the minimum.
Choosing $\Theta(\log n)$ by thinking the maximum can be found by walking one path, as in deleting the minimum. There is no path that leads to the maximum, since it can be at any leaf.
Choosing $\Theta(n \log n)$ by sorting the heap first. Sorting is far more work than needed, and a plain scan of the leaves already gives $O(n)$.

recognize.clues: The heap is a min-heap but the question asks for the maximum. The words worst case and optimal algorithm point to a lower-bound argument, not to a root or path operation.
recognize.contrast: Not the standard heap operations: reading the minimum is constant and deleting it follows one path in logarithmic time. The maximum of a min-heap has no path leading to it.

check.body: Test with a small min-heap array, 1, 3, 2, 7, 5, 4, 6 (positions 1 to 7). The leaves are positions 4 to 7 and hold 7, 5, 4, 6, and the maximum 7 is among them. Swap 7 and 4 and the array is still a valid min-heap, yet the maximum moved, so an algorithm that skipped a leaf could be fooled.

questions.stem:
Consider a complete binary tree with 7 nodes. Let $A$ denote the set of first 3 elements obtained by performing Breadth-First Search (BFS) starting from the root. Let $B$ denote the set of first 3 elements obtained by performing Depth-First Search (DFS) starting from the root.
The value of $|A - B|$ is _____________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Complete binary tree with 7 nodes numbered 1 to 7 level by level: BFS visits 1, 2, 3 first; DFS visits 1, 2, 4 first; the set A is {1,2,3}, the set B is {1,2,4}, so A minus B is {3} and its size is 1

steps.title: The two searches, in plain words
steps.body: A complete binary tree with 7 nodes has every level full: 1 node at the root, 2 children, and 4 grandchildren (leaves). Breadth-First Search (BFS) visits the root, then all nodes one step away, then all nodes two steps away, so it goes level by level and uses a queue. Depth-First Search (DFS) goes as deep as it can along one branch before coming back, so after the root it visits a child and then that child's own child. $A - B$ is the set of elements in $A$ that are not in $B$, and $|A - B|$ is how many there are. Number the nodes 1 to 7 level by level, left to right.
steps.tex: A - B = \{x : x \in A,\ x \notin B\}

steps.title: The set A
steps.body: BFS visits the root 1 first. The next nodes are its two children, 2 and 3. So the first three are 1, 2, 3 and $A = \{1, 2, 3\}$.

steps.title: The set B
steps.body: DFS visits 1, then goes into one child, say the left child 2, then into the child of 2 on the left, which is 4. So the first three are 1, 2, 4 and $B = \{1, 2, 4\}$. If DFS tries the right child first, it gives 1, 3, 7 instead.

steps.title: The difference
steps.body: With the left-first order, $A - B = \{1,2,3\} - \{1,2,4\} = \{3\}$, so $|A - B| = 1$. With the right-first order, $B = \{1, 3, 7\}$ and $A - B = \{2\}$, which also has size 1. The order in which DFS tries the children does not change the answer. The answer is 1.

shortcut.body: The first three of BFS are the root and both its children. The first three of DFS are the root, a child and a grandchild. They share the root and one child; each has exactly one node the other lacks. So $|A - B| = 1$ for any complete tree with at least 7 nodes.

traps.text: Answering 0 by thinking both searches start the same way and so give the same first three. BFS takes both children of the root; DFS takes only one child and then a grandchild.
Answering 2, the size of the symmetric difference $\{3\} \cup \{4\}$. The question asks for $A - B$, which counts only elements of $A$ missing from $B$.
Answering 3 by counting all elements of $A$ as different from $B$. The root 1 and the child 2 are in both sets.

recognize.clues: Two searches, BFS and DFS, are compared on the first few nodes visited from the root of a complete binary tree, with a set difference on the results.
recognize.contrast: Not a full-traversal question: only the opening of each search matters. The difference from level-order and preorder is only how the third node is chosen.

check.body: Repeat with DFS trying the right child first: it visits 1, 3, 7, so $B = \{1, 3, 7\}$ and $A - B = \{2\}$, again one element. A second route is to count: $A$ has 3 elements, and exactly 2 of them (the root and one child) also appear in $B$, so 1 is left over.

questions.stem: A binary search tree $T$ contains $n$ distinct elements. What is the time complexity of picking an element in $T$ that is smaller than the maximum element in $T$?

solutionDiagram.alt: Left: BST whose root 50 has a right child, so 50 is smaller than the maximum 70 and the answer is the root; right: BST whose root 90 has no right child, so 90 is the maximum and its left child 40 is smaller

steps.title: The terms, and what the question really asks
steps.body: A binary search tree (BST) keeps every key of the left subtree below its node and every key of the right subtree above it. The maximum of a BST is the node you reach by following right pointers until there is none. The question does not ask for the maximum. It asks for any one element that is smaller than the maximum, and at least one exists once $n \ge 2$. A node that has a right child is always smaller than something, because the right subtree holds larger keys.

steps.title: Case 1: the root has a right child
steps.body: Every key in the right subtree is larger than the root, so the root is not the maximum and it is smaller than the maximum. Return the root. In the left drawing, the root 50 has the right child 70, and the maximum is 80, so 50 qualifies. This took one test.

steps.title: Case 2: the root has no right child
steps.body: Then nothing is larger than the root, so the root is the maximum. All other keys are in the left subtree, which is not empty because $n \ge 2$. Its root, the left child of the root, is smaller than the maximum. Return the left child. In the right drawing the root is 90, and its left child 40 is the answer. This took one test and one pointer read.

steps.title: Cost
steps.body: In both cases the work is one pointer test and at most one pointer read, whatever $n$ is. The cost is $\Theta(1)$, which is option D. Finding the maximum itself would cost the height of the tree, which is why the question is a trap for anyone who goes looking for it.

shortcut.body: Any element except the maximum will do, and the root is not the maximum unless it has no right child. Check the root, and otherwise use its left child. Two lookups, $\Theta(1)$. Unsafe for $n = 1$, where no smaller element exists.

traps.text: Choosing $\Theta(n \log n)$ by sorting the tree. Sorting is unnecessary; no search is needed at all.
Choosing $\Theta(n)$ by scanning every node to find the maximum and then picking another. You do not need the maximum, only a key below it.

Choosing $\Theta(\log n)$ because finding the maximum of a BST takes a walk down the right spine. The question asks for something smaller than the maximum, which the root or its left child supplies at once.

recognize.clues: The words picking an element smaller than the maximum, not finding the maximum. Any one valid element is enough, so the BST ordering can be used at the root.
recognize.contrast: Not the maximum query, which walks the right spine in time proportional to the height. Asking for any element below the maximum is looser and needs no walk.

check.body: Test the smallest case $n = 2$. If the root has a right child, return the root, which is smaller than that child. If not, the second key is the left child, smaller than the root. Both give a valid element after one test, so the cost cannot grow with the size of the tree.
