questions.stem: The preorder traversal of a binary search tree is 15, 10, 12, 11, 20, 18, 16, 19. Which one of the following is the postorder traversal of the tree?

solutionDiagram.alt: BST rebuilt from the preorder 15 10 12 11 20 18 16 19 with each node's postorder position beside it: 11 is 1, 12 is 2, 10 is 3, 16 is 4, 19 is 5, 18 is 6, 20 is 7, 15 is 8

steps.title: The three traversals and the rule that rebuilds a BST
steps.body: A traversal lists the nodes in a fixed order. Preorder is node, left subtree, right subtree. Postorder is left subtree, right subtree, node. Inorder is left subtree, node, right subtree. In a binary search tree (BST) every key in the left subtree is smaller than the node and every key in the right subtree is larger. The rebuilding rule is: the first key of a preorder list is the root; the keys after it that are smaller than the root form the left subtree, and the keys that are larger form the right subtree, and the same rule applies inside each part.

steps.title: Split at the root 15
steps.body: The root is 15. The keys after it that are smaller than 15 are 10, 12, 11. The keys larger than 15 are 20, 18, 16, 19. So 10, 12, 11 is the left subtree and 20, 18, 16, 19 is the right subtree.

steps.title: Rebuild the left subtree
steps.body: In 10, 12, 11 the root is 10. Nothing is smaller, so the left child is empty; 12 and 11 are larger and form the right subtree. In 12, 11 the root is 12 and 11 is smaller, so 11 is the left child of 12. The left subtree is 10, whose right child is 12, whose left child is 11.

steps.title: Rebuild the right subtree
steps.body: In 20, 18, 16, 19 the root is 20 and everything else is smaller, so all of 18, 16, 19 is the left subtree. In 18, 16, 19 the root is 18, with 16 on the left and 19 on the right. The right subtree is 20 whose left child is 18, which has children 16 and 19.

steps.title: Postorder: left, right, node
steps.body: Postorder of the left subtree: 11 (leaf), 12, then 10, giving 11, 12, 10. Postorder of the right subtree: 16, 19, then 18, then 20, giving 16, 19, 18, 20. Then the root. The postorder is 11, 12, 10, 16, 19, 18, 20, 15, which is option B.

shortcut.body: Postorder always ends with the root, so the last key must be 15, which keeps B and D. Postorder of a BST puts the keys of the left subtree first, and 11, 12, 10 belongs to the left part, so B. Unsafe: elimination by the last key alone leaves two options.

traps.text: Choosing A: the keys in sorted order are the inorder traversal, not the postorder. A BST's inorder is always sorted.
Choosing C: this is the sorted order reversed (right, node, left), which is not any of the three standard traversals.
Choosing D: this visits the right subtree before the left subtree, a mirror of postorder. Postorder must read the left subtree first.

recognize.clues: A preorder sequence of a binary search tree is given and a different traversal is asked for. The BST property, smaller to the left and larger to the right, is what makes the tree unique.
recognize.contrast: Not the case of two traversals of a general tree. Here one traversal plus the BST order is enough, because the inorder is the sorted list of the keys.

check.body: Sort the keys to get the inorder, 10, 11, 12, 15, 16, 18, 19, 20. Preorder and inorder together fix the tree, and the postorder must end with the root 15 and must put every key of the left part, 10, 11, 12, before the right part. A candidate postorder that fails either test is wrong.

questions.stem: What is the worst case time complexity of inserting $n^2$ elements into an AVL-tree with $n$ elements initially?

steps.title: AVL tree, height, and the cost of one insertion
steps.body: An AVL tree is a binary search tree in which, at every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. That keeps the height within a constant factor of $\log_2$ of the number of nodes: a tree with $m$ nodes has height $\Theta(\log m)$. To insert a key you walk from the root down to the empty place where it belongs (at most height steps), attach it, and walk back up fixing any imbalance; a fix is one or two rotations, each costing $O(1)$. So one insertion into a tree of $m$ nodes costs $\Theta(\log m)$ in the worst case.

steps.title: The sizes while the n squared keys go in
steps.body: The tree starts with $n$ nodes and grows to $n + n^2$. The $i$-th insertion happens in a tree of $n + i - 1$ nodes, so it costs $\Theta(\log(n+i))$. The total is the sum of these costs for $i = 1, \ldots, n^2$.

steps.title: Upper bound
steps.body: Every tree along the way has at most $n + n^2 \le 2n^2$ nodes, so each insertion costs at most $c \log_2 (2n^2) = c(2\log_2 n + 1)$, which is $O(\log n)$. There are $n^2$ insertions, so the total is $O(n^2 \log n)$.

steps.title: Lower bound
steps.body: After the first half of the insertions, the tree holds more than $n^2/2$ nodes, so its height is at least $\log_2 (n^2/2) = 2\log_2 n - 1$. An adversary can always choose a key that falls under the deepest leaf, so each of the last $n^2/2$ insertions costs at least about $2 \log_2 n - 1$. The total is $\Omega(n^2 \log n)$. A numeric check agrees: the ratio of $\sum \log_2 (n+i)$ to $n^2 \log_2 n$ is 1.72, 1.80, 1.86 and 1.88 for $n = 10, 100, 1000, 3000$, creeping toward 2, a constant. The answer is $\Theta(n^2 \log n)$, option C.

shortcut.body: Count the insertions ($n^2$) and multiply by the cost of one, a walk down a balanced tree: $\log(n^2) = 2\log n$. That gives $n^2 \cdot \Theta(\log n)$. Unsafe if you forget that the cost per insertion depends on the height, not on the size.

traps.text: Choosing $\Theta(n^4)$ by charging each insertion the size of the tree, about $n^2$, as if the tree were a list. An AVL tree is balanced, so an insertion costs the height, not the size.
Choosing $\Theta(n^2)$ by treating one insertion as $O(1)$ because a rotation costs $O(1)$. The search for the place to insert still walks down the tree.
Choosing $\Theta(n^3)$ by charging each of the $n^2$ insertions the starting size $n$. The cost depends on $\log$ of the size, not on the size.

recognize.clues: A worst case total over many insertions into an AVL tree, with the number of insertions given as a function of the starting size. The key is that height is logarithmic in size.
recognize.contrast: Not a single-insertion question and not an unbalanced BST, where each insertion could cost the full size of the tree. The balance rule is what caps the cost per insertion.

check.body: Test numerically. For $n = 10$ and $n = 100$, add up $\log_2(n+i)$ for $i$ from 1 to $n^2$ and divide by $n^2 \log_2 n$. The ratios settle near a constant (about 1.7 to 1.9 for these sizes), so the total grows like $n^2 \log n$ and not like $n^2$ or $n^3$.

questions.stem: In a balanced binary search tree with $n$ elements, what is the worst case time complexity of reporting all elements in range $[a, b]$? Assume that the number of reported elements is $k$.

solutionDiagram.alt: Balanced BST on keys 1 to 15 queried for the range 5 to 11: reported nodes 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 are thick, nodes 4 and 12 are visited but not reported (dashed), and the subtrees under 2 and 14 are never entered

steps.title: Balanced BST, range query, and the rule that prunes
steps.body: A binary search tree (BST) keeps smaller keys on the left and larger keys on the right, and a balanced one has height $\Theta(\log n)$. A range query reports every key $x$ with $a \le x \le b$. At a node $x$ there are three cases, and they decide everything. If $x < a$, no key in its left subtree can qualify, so go right only. If $x > b$, no key in its right subtree can qualify, so go left only. If $a \le x \le b$, report $x$ and continue into both subtrees.
steps.tex: x<a:\ \text{go right};\qquad x>b:\ \text{go left};\qquad a\le x\le b:\ \text{report, go both}

steps.title: Run it on 15 keys
steps.body: Take the balanced tree on the keys 1 to 15 (root 8) and the range $[5, 11]$. The root 8 is in range: report it, go both ways. Node 4 is below 5: go right only to 6, so its left subtree (2, 1, 3) is never entered. Node 6 is in range: report it and its children 5 and 7. On the other side node 12 is above 11: go left only to 10, so 14, 13 and 15 are never entered. Node 10 is in range: report it and its children 9 and 11. Reported: $8, 6, 5, 7, 10, 9, 11$, which is $k = 7$ keys. Visited but not reported: 4 and 12. So 9 nodes are visited.

steps.title: Count the work in general
steps.body: Every visited node is either reported, which adds up to $k$, or not reported. A node that is visited and not reported is below $a$ or above $b$, so it lies on the search path towards $a$ or towards $b$. Those are two root-to-leaf paths, each of length at most the height $\Theta(\log n)$. Visits are at most $k + 2\log n$ up to a constant, so the cost is $O(\log n + k)$.

steps.title: The bound is tight
steps.body: Even when $k = 0$ the search must go down a path to find where $a$ would be, which takes $\Omega(\log n)$. And reporting $k$ keys takes $\Omega(k)$ steps. So the worst case is $\Theta(\log n + k)$, option B.

shortcut.body: Test the extreme cases against the options. With $k = 0$ the answer must still be about $\log n$, since the search has to find where the range would be. With $k = n$ the answer must be about $n$, since $n$ keys are printed. Only $\Theta(\log n + k)$ fits both. Option A fails at $k = n$, option C gives $n \log n$ and D gives $n \log n$ at $k = n$.

traps.text: Choosing $\Theta(\log n)$: this is the cost of finding one key. Reporting $k$ keys costs at least $k$ steps just to print them.
Choosing $\Theta(k \log n)$ by running a fresh search for each reported key. Consecutive keys are found by walking the tree, not by searching from the root again.
Choosing $\Theta(n \log k)$: nothing in the algorithm touches all $n$ nodes, because the pruning rule skips every subtree that lies outside the range.

recognize.clues: A balanced BST and a range of keys, with the output size $k$ given as a parameter. The cost is expected to depend on both the tree size and the number of keys reported.
recognize.contrast: Not a search for one key, which costs only the height, and not a full scan, which costs $n$. Range reporting prunes whole subtrees, so the cost is the height plus the output size.

check.body: Run a different range on the same 15-key tree: $[9, 9]$. The search visits 8, 12, 10 and 9, and only 9 is reported. The three other visits lie on the single path down to the range, so the cost is the reported keys plus a path of length about $\log n$.

questions.stem: Consider the array representation of a binary min-heap containing 1023 elements. The minimum number of comparisons required to find the maximum in the heap is _____________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Min-heap of 15 values with the 8 leaves thick, and a knockout bracket over the 8 leaves: 4 plus 2 plus 1 equals 7 comparisons, which is leaves minus 1; for 1023 elements there are 512 leaves and 511 comparisons

steps.title: Min-heap and leaves
steps.body: A binary min-heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array where every parent is smaller than or equal to its children. A leaf is a node with no children, and in an array of $n$ elements the leaves are the nodes with index above $n/2$. With $n = 1023 = 2^{10} - 1$ the tree has exactly 10 full levels. The internal nodes are the first $511$ and the leaves are the last $512$ (indices 512 to 1023).

steps.title: The maximum is at a leaf
steps.body: An internal node has a child at least as large as itself, so the maximum value can always be read at a leaf. That narrows the search to 512 values. The heap rule says nothing about two leaves, so these 512 values are in no known order: the drawing shows a 15-key heap whose 8 leaves are 15, 9, 8, 11, 12, 14, 10, 13, arbitrary against each other.

steps.title: Lower bound: 511 comparisons
steps.body: Start with 512 candidates for the maximum. A comparison of two values removes at most one candidate, the smaller one. To end with a single candidate the algorithm must remove 511, so it needs at least 511 comparisons. No algorithm that compares keys can do better.

steps.title: Upper bound and the answer
steps.body: A knockout tournament matches the leaves in pairs: $256 + 128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 511$ comparisons, and the winner is the maximum. The drawing shows the same idea for 8 leaves: $4 + 2 + 1 = 7 = 8 - 1$. The answer is 511.

shortcut.body: Leaves $=(n+1)/2 = 512$ for $n = 1023$. Finding the maximum of $L$ unordered values needs $L - 1$ comparisons, so $512 - 1 = 511$. Unsafe if the heap is not full: use the number of leaves $n - \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ and subtract one.

traps.text: Answering 1022, which is $n - 1$: it ignores the heap and compares all 1023 elements. The structure lets you skip every internal node.
Answering 512, the number of leaves. A tournament over 512 values takes one fewer comparison than values.
Answering 0 or 1 by thinking the maximum is at the root. That holds for a max-heap; in a min-heap the root is the minimum.

recognize.clues: A min-heap stored in an array with 1023 elements, and a question about the maximum, which is the end the heap does not order. The count $1023 = 2^{10} - 1$ fixes how many leaves there are.
recognize.contrast: Not extract-min or insert, which use the heap order and cost $O(\log n)$. The minimum is free at the root, but the maximum forces a scan of the unordered leaves.

check.body: Try a heap of 7 keys: the leaves are the indices 4 to 7, which is 4 keys, and a knockout among 4 unordered values takes 3 comparisons. Scanning all 7 keys would take 6, so looking only at the leaves is what makes the count smaller. The same rule for 15 keys gives 7 comparisons, which matches the 8-leaf drawing.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements:
I. The smallest element in a max-heap is always at a leaf node
II. The second largest element in a max-heap is always a child of the root node
III. A max-heap can be constructed from a binary search tree in $\Theta(n)$ time
IV. A binary search tree can be constructed from a max-heap in $\Theta(n)$ time

Which of the above statements are TRUE?

solutionDiagram.alt: Max-heap with root 50, children 30 and 40, then 10, 20, 35, 25: the smallest value 10 is at a leaf and the second largest 40 is a child of the root; statements I, II and III are true and IV is false

steps.title: The structures and the one fact about sorting that is needed
steps.body: A max-heap is a complete binary tree in which every parent is at least as large as its children, so the maximum is at the root. A leaf is a node with no children. A binary search tree (BST) keeps smaller keys on the left and larger keys on the right, so its inorder traversal (left, node, right) lists the keys in increasing order. Any method that sorts $n$ keys by comparing them needs $\Omega(n \log n)$ comparisons in the worst case, so no comparison method can sort in $\Theta(n)$ time. A max-heap can be built from any $n$ keys in $\Theta(n)$ time, a fact used in statement IV.

steps.title: Statement I: true
steps.body: An internal node has a child that is no larger than itself. So an internal node cannot be strictly the smallest: the smallest key is found at a leaf, as the thick leaf 10 in the drawing (the tree has root 50, children 30 and 40, and leaves 10, 20, 35, 25). If there are ties, the same value also appears at a leaf.

steps.title: Statement II: true
steps.body: The root is the maximum. Every other key lies in the subtree of one of the root's two children, and the largest key of a subtree is its own root, because the heap rule puts the maximum of a subtree at its root. So the second largest key is the larger of the two children. In the drawing it is 40.

steps.title: Statement III: true
steps.body: Run an inorder traversal of the BST, which costs $\Theta(n)$ and produces the keys in increasing order. Write them into an array in decreasing order (fill from the back). In a descending array every parent index is smaller than its child index, so every parent is larger than its children, and the array is a max-heap. The total is $\Theta(n)$.

steps.title: Statement IV: false
steps.body: Suppose a BST could be built from a max-heap in $\Theta(n)$ time. Then any $n$ keys could be sorted in $\Theta(n)$: build the heap in $\Theta(n)$, convert it to a BST in $\Theta(n)$, and read the BST in inorder in $\Theta(n)$. That would beat the $\Omega(n \log n)$ lower bound. So IV is false. I, II and III are true: option A.

shortcut.body: Statement IV is the quick elimination: it would sort in linear time. Options B, C and D all contain IV, so only A remains. Takes about 30 seconds. Unsafe if you doubt I, II, III, but the options leave no room for that.

traps.text: Choosing B because a heap looks nearly sorted, so turning it into a BST feels cheap. A BST encodes the full sorted order, and a linear-time conversion would break the $\Omega(n \log n)$ sorting bound.

Choosing C because the second largest key looks as if it could sit deeper in the tree. It cannot: everything below the root is under one of its two children, and each child is the largest of its own subtree.
Choosing D because the smallest key looks as if it could be at the root's level, as in a min-heap. In a max-heap the smallest key is at the bottom. Statement IV also makes D false.

recognize.clues: Four true or false claims about a max-heap and a BST, with the words smallest, second largest and $\Theta(n)$ conversion. These point at the heap order and at the comparison-sorting lower bound.
recognize.contrast: Not heap construction by repeated insertion, which costs $\Theta(n \log n)$; building from an array is $\Theta(n)$. Going from a BST to a heap only reads an already sorted order, while going the other way would need sorting.

check.body: Test the first two claims on the max-heap with level order 9, 7, 8, 1, 3, 2, 4. The smallest key 1 is a leaf, and the second largest key 8 is a child of the root. For III, take the BST with root 2 and children 1, 3: its inorder is 1, 2, 3, and writing that in descending order gives the array 3, 2, 1, which is a max-heap, found in one linear pass. For IV, a linear conversion from a heap to a BST would sort in linear time, since building the heap is linear and reading the BST inorder is linear, which contradicts the sorting bound.

questions.stem: Let $T$ be a full binary tree with 8 leaves. (A full binary tree has every level full.) Suppose two leaves $a$ and $b$ of $T$ are chosen uniformly and independently at random. The expected value of the distance between $a$ and $b$ in $T$ (i.e., the number of edges in the unique path between $a$ and $b$) is (rounded off to 2 decimal places) _____________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Perfect binary tree with 8 leaves L1 to L8; distances from leaf L1 to L1..L8 are 0, 2, 4, 4, 6, 6, 6, 6, sum 34, so the expected distance over 64 equally likely ordered pairs is 34/8 = 4.25

steps.title: The tree, the distance, and what independent means
steps.body: A full binary tree in this question has every level full, so with 8 leaves it is the perfect tree with levels of 1, 2, 4 and 8 nodes: three edges from the root to each leaf. The distance between two leaves is the number of edges on the path between them, and that path climbs from each leaf to their lowest common ancestor (LCA) and goes down again. If the LCA is $j$ levels above the leaves, the distance is $2j$. Choosing $a$ and $b$ independently means all $8 \times 8 = 64$ ordered pairs are equally likely, and $b = a$ is allowed, with distance 0.
steps.tex: d(a,b) = 2j,\quad j = \text{height of the LCA above the leaves}

steps.title: Fix a leaf a and list the 8 choices of b
steps.body: Take $a = L_1$ (the leftmost leaf). If $b = L_1$, the distance is 0 (1 leaf). If $b = L_2$, the sibling, the LCA is the parent, one level up, and the distance is 2 (1 leaf). If $b \in \{L_3, L_4\}$, the LCA is two levels up and the distance is 4 (2 leaves). If $b \in \{L_5, \ldots, L_8\}$, the LCA is the root, three levels up, and the distance is 6 (4 leaves).

steps.title: Sum and divide
steps.body: The distances from $L_1$ add up to $0 + 2 + 4 + 4 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 34$. Every leaf sees the same pattern by symmetry, so the average over $b$ is $34/8$ for every $a$, and the expectation over all 64 pairs is the same.

steps.title: Check with probabilities
steps.body: The LCA is at height 0 with probability $1/8$, height 1 with $1/8$, height 2 with $2/8$ and height 3 with $4/8$. So $E = 2\,(1\cdot\tfrac18 + 2\cdot\tfrac28 + 3\cdot\tfrac48) = 2 \cdot 17/8 = 4.25$. The answer is 4.25.

shortcut.body: The distance is twice the height of the LCA above the leaves. Half the time the two leaves are in different halves of the tree (LCA at the root, distance 6), a quarter of the time in different quarters (distance 4), and so on: $E = 6\cdot\tfrac12 + 4\cdot\tfrac14 + 2\cdot\tfrac18 + 0 \cdot \tfrac18 = 4.25$. Unsafe if you forget that $a = b$ is allowed.

traps.text: Answering 4.86, which is $34/7$: it divides by 7 because it removes the case $b = a$. The question says the leaves are chosen independently, so $b = a$ has probability $1/8$ and distance 0.
Answering 5.25, which is 4.25 + 1: it counts the nodes on the path instead of the edges.
Answering 6, which sends every path through the root. Only half of the choices of $b$ lie in the other half of the tree.

recognize.clues: A full binary tree with 8 leaves in which every level is full, two leaves picked independently and an expected path length. The perfect shape gives equal depths, and independence allows the same leaf twice.
recognize.contrast: Not a counting-trees question: the tree is fixed and only the pair of leaves is random.

check.body: Use a second route, a recurrence. Split the leaves by the two halves under the root. With probability $1/2$ both lie in the same half, a perfect tree with half the leaves, so the expected distance is $E(L)$. With probability $1/2$ they lie in different halves and the path passes through the root, so the distance is $2(d+1)$ for leaf depth $d+1$ in the full tree, where $d = \log_2 L$. This gives $E(2L) = E(L)/2 + (d+1)$. From $E(2) = 1$: $E(4) = 1/2 + 2 = 2.5$, which matches the direct count 0, 2, 4, 4. Then $E(8) = 2.5/2 + 3 = 4.25$, the same value as the main route.

questions.stem: The postorder traversal of a binary tree is 8, 9, 6, 7, 4, 5, 2, 3, 1. The inorder traversal of the same tree is 8, 6, 9, 4, 7, 2, 5, 1, 3. The height of a tree is the length of the longest path from the root to any leaf. The height of the binary tree above is _____________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Binary tree rebuilt from postorder 8 9 6 7 4 5 2 3 1 and inorder 8 6 9 4 7 2 5 1 3: root 1, left child 2 with children 4 and 5, 4 has children 6 and 7, 6 has children 8 and 9, and 1 has right child 3; the longest path 1, 2, 4, 6, 8 has 4 edges

steps.title: Postorder, inorder, and the rule that rebuilds the tree
steps.body: Postorder lists a tree as left subtree, right subtree, node. Inorder lists it as left subtree, node, right subtree. The height is the number of edges on the longest path from the root down to a leaf (a single node has height 0). The rule: the last key of a postorder list is the root. In the inorder list, the keys to the left of the root belong to the left subtree and the keys to the right of it belong to the right subtree. The postorder list of a subtree is the matching piece of the postorder list, in the same order.

steps.title: The root and the first split
steps.body: The last postorder key is 1, so the root is 1. In the inorder list 8, 6, 9, 4, 7, 2, 5, 1, 3 the keys before 1 are 8, 6, 9, 4, 7, 2, 5 (7 keys, the left subtree) and the key after it is 3 (the right subtree, a single node). The left subtree has the postorder 8, 9, 6, 7, 4, 5, 2, the first 7 keys.

steps.title: Follow the left side down
steps.body: The last key of 8, 9, 6, 7, 4, 5, 2 is 2, so 2 is the left child of 1. In the inorder 8, 6, 9, 4, 7, 2, 5 the keys before 2 are 8, 6, 9, 4, 7 and after it only 5. So 5 is the right child of 2, and the left part has postorder 8, 9, 6, 7, 4. Its last key 4 is the root of that part. In the inorder 8, 6, 9, 4, 7 the keys before 4 are 8, 6, 9 and after it only 7. So 4 has the right child 7 and the left part 8, 6, 9 with postorder 8, 9, 6. Its root is 6, and in the inorder 8, 6, 9 the key 8 is left of 6 and 9 is right of it.

steps.title: The tree and its height
steps.body: The tree is: 1 with the children 2 and 3; 2 with the children 4 and 5; 4 with the children 6 and 7; 6 with the children 8 and 9. The longest path is 1, 2, 4, 6, 8 (or 9), which has 5 nodes and 4 edges. The height is 4.

shortcut.body: You do not need the whole tree. Every time the left part is non-empty the new root is the last key of its postorder piece, so follow the roots down the left spine: 1, 2, 4, 6, 8. That is 5 nodes, so 4 edges. Unsafe if the longest path turns out to be on the right side; here the right pieces are single nodes (3, 5, 7).

traps.text: Answering 5, which counts the nodes on the longest path. The height counts edges, so a path of 5 nodes has height 4.
Answering 3 or 2 from the shorter side: the right side of the root is the single leaf 3, but the height is taken from the longest path, the one through 2, 4 and 6.
Answering 9, the number of nodes. That would be the height only for a chain, and this tree branches at 1, 2, 4 and 6.

recognize.clues: A postorder and an inorder list of the same tree are both given, and the question asks a property of the whole tree, its height. An inorder list together with a postorder list fixes exactly one tree.
recognize.contrast: Preorder with postorder does not fix a tree, and counting-trees asks how many trees fit a description. Here the two lists pin down one tree, so rebuilding it is safe.

check.body: Read the tree you built back out. Its inorder walk must be 8, 6, 9, 4, 7, 2, 5, 1, 3 and its postorder walk must be 8, 9, 6, 7, 4, 5, 2, 3, 1. A tree that reproduces both lists is the only one that can exist, so the height read from it is the answer.

questions.stem: The number of possible min-heaps containing each value from $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7\}$ exactly once is _____________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Min-heap of 7 values: the root is 1, the other 6 values are split into a left group of 3 and a right group of 3 in C(6,3) = 20 ways, and each group of 3 forms a min-heap in 2 ways, 20 times 2 times 2 equals 80

steps.title: What is being counted
steps.body: A min-heap is a complete binary tree in which every parent is smaller than its children. With 7 nodes the shape is forced: the root, two children, and four grandchildren, so 3 full levels. Two min-heaps are different if some position holds a different value. So the question is how many ways the values 1 to 7 can be placed in that fixed shape so that every parent is smaller than its children.

steps.title: The root is forced
steps.body: Every node is below the root, so the root is smaller than all the rest. The root must hold 1. The other six values go into the two subtrees, each a 3-node tree (a node with two children).

steps.title: Choose which three go left
steps.body: Pick the 3 values (out of the remaining 6) that go into the left subtree. The other 3 go into the right subtree. The number of ways to choose them is $\binom{6}{3} = 20$. The drawing shows the root 1 above two triangles of 3 values each.

steps.title: Arrange each group of three
steps.body: A 3-node subtree on values $x < y < z$ must have $x$ on top, because the top is smaller than both children. The two children $y$ and $z$ can go in either order, so there are 2 heaps. Each of the two subtrees has 2 choices, independent of the other.

steps.title: Multiply
steps.body: The total is the choice of the group times the arrangement of each group: $20 \times 2 \times 2 = 80$. A direct count over all 5040 orders of the seven values gives the same 80.

shortcut.body: Root forced (1 way), split the other six into two groups of three ($\binom63 = 20$), and each group of three has $2$ orders: $20 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 80$. Unsafe if the shape is not forced: for other sizes the left and right sizes must follow the complete-tree shape.

traps.text: Answering 20: it counts only the choice of the left group and forgets that the two children of each group can be swapped.
Answering 40: it counts the two orders for one group only. Each of the two groups of three has its own factor 2.
Answering 140, which is $\binom{7}{3}\cdot 4$: it picks the left group from all seven values. The root takes 1 first, so only six values are left to split.

recognize.clues: The question counts min-heaps over seven distinct values, so the shape is forced and only the placement of values varies. Seven nodes fill exactly three levels.
recognize.contrast: Not counting-trees, which counts tree shapes. Here the shape is fixed by completeness and the count is over value placements.

check.body: Run the same method on smaller sets and compare with a hand listing. For {1, 2, 3} the root is 1 and the two children can swap, so 2 heaps. For {1, 2, 3, 4} the left subtree has two nodes and the right one, giving $\binom{3}{2} \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = 3$ heaps, and listing the arrays by hand also finds 3.

questions.stem: The pre-order traversal of a binary search tree is given by 12, 8, 6, 2, 7, 9, 10, 16, 15, 19, 17, 20. Then the post-order traversal of this tree is:

solutionDiagram.alt: BST rebuilt from the preorder 12 8 6 2 7 9 10 16 15 19 17 20 with each node's postorder position beside it: 2 is 1, 7 is 2, 6 is 3, 10 is 4, 9 is 5, 8 is 6, 15 is 7, 17 is 8, 20 is 9, 19 is 10, 16 is 11, 12 is 12

steps.title: Preorder, postorder, and the rule that rebuilds a BST
steps.body: Preorder lists a tree as node, left subtree, right subtree; postorder lists it as left subtree, right subtree, node. In a binary search tree (BST) every key in the left subtree is smaller than the node, and every key in the right subtree is larger. So the first key of a preorder list is the root, the keys after it that are smaller form the left subtree, the next larger keys form the right subtree, and the rule repeats inside each part.

steps.title: The left side of the root 12
steps.body: After 12, the keys smaller than 12 are 8, 6, 2, 7, 9, 10 (the left subtree) and the larger keys are 16, 15, 19, 17, 20 (the right subtree). In 8, 6, 2, 7, 9, 10 the root is 8; the smaller keys 6, 2, 7 are its left subtree and the larger keys 9, 10 are its right subtree. In 6, 2, 7 the root is 6, with 2 on the left and 7 on the right. In 9, 10 the root is 9 and 10 is its right child.

steps.title: The right side of the root 12
steps.body: In 16, 15, 19, 17, 20 the root is 16; the smaller key 15 is its left child and 19, 17, 20 is its right subtree. In 19, 17, 20 the root is 19, with 17 on the left and 20 on the right.

steps.title: Read the postorder
steps.body: Left subtree of 8: 2, 7, 6. Right subtree of 8: 10, 9. Then 8. That gives 2, 7, 6, 10, 9, 8 for the left subtree of 12. For the right subtree of 12: 15 (the left child), then 17, 20, 19, then 16, giving 15, 17, 20, 19, 16. Then the root 12. The postorder is 2, 7, 6, 10, 9, 8, 15, 17, 20, 19, 16, 12, which is option B. The drawing numbers each node by its position in this list.

shortcut.body: Postorder ends with the root 12 in all options, so look at the start: the first key in postorder is the leftmost leaf. Following the left spine of the preorder 12, 8, 6, 2 gives the leaf 2, and its sibling 7 must come right after it. Only B starts 2, 7. Unsafe if only the first two keys are compared.

traps.text: Choosing A: it is the sorted list. That is the inorder traversal of a BST, not the postorder.
Choosing C: it starts with 7 before 2, so the right child 7 appears before its left sibling 2. Postorder reads the left subtree first.
Choosing D: it starts with 7, 6, 2, which reads the subtree of 6 as right, node, left. Postorder is left, right, node.

recognize.clues: The preorder of a binary search tree is given and the postorder is asked. The words binary search tree matter: they supply the ordering that a preorder list alone does not carry.
recognize.contrast: For a general binary tree a preorder list does not fix the tree, and the inorder list is needed as well. For a BST the sorted keys are the inorder list, so it is implied.

check.body: In a correct postorder, every node appears after both of its children. From the preorder, 6 has children 2 and 7, 9 has the right child 10, and 16 has children 15 and 19. Check that in the list you chose, 2 and 7 come before 6, 10 comes before 9, and 15 and 19 come before 16.

questions.stem:
Let $T$ be a binary search tree with 15 nodes. The minimum and maximum possible heights of $T$ are:
Note: The height of a tree with a single node is 0.

solutionDiagram.alt: Left: a perfect binary tree with 15 nodes has height 3, the smallest possible; right: a chain of 15 nodes, each with a single child, has height 14, the largest possible

steps.title: Height, and why a BST of 15 nodes can have many shapes
steps.body: The height of a tree is the number of edges on its longest path from the root to a leaf, so a single node has height 0 (the question says so). The level of a node is its distance from the root: the root is on level 0. The shape of a binary search tree (BST) depends on the order in which the keys were inserted, so the same 15 keys can make a thin tree or a bushy tree. We want the smallest and largest height over all shapes.
steps.tex: \text{height} = \text{number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path}

steps.title: Maximum height: a chain
steps.body: Each level has at least one node on it, or the tree would have stopped. With 15 nodes there are at most 15 levels, numbered 0 to 14, so the height is at most 14. Inserting the keys 1, 2, ..., 15 in increasing order makes every new key the right child of the last one, a chain with 14 edges. The maximum height is $n - 1 = 14$.

steps.title: Minimum height: a perfect tree
steps.body: Level $d$ holds at most $2^d$ nodes, so a tree of height $h$ holds at most $1 + 2 + 4 + \cdots + 2^h = 2^{h+1} - 1$ nodes. We need room for 15 nodes: $2^{h+1} - 1 \ge 15$ gives $2^{h+1} \ge 16$, so $h \ge 3$. Height 3 is reached: put the middle key 8 at the root, 4 and 12 below it, and so on, to get a full tree with levels of 1, 2, 4, 8 nodes, which has exactly 15 nodes. The minimum height is 3.

steps.title: The answer
steps.body: The minimum is 3 and the maximum is 14, which is option B. The drawing shows the perfect tree on the left and the 15-node chain on the right.

shortcut.body: Minimum $= \lceil \log_2 (n+1) \rceil - 1 = \lceil \log_2 16 \rceil - 1 = 3$ and maximum $= n - 1 = 14$. Take care that the question counts edges: a single node has height 0.

traps.text: Choosing 4 and 15: this counts levels (or nodes on the path) instead of edges, so both numbers are one too large. The note says a single node has height 0.
Choosing 4 and 14: the maximum of 14 is right, but a minimum of 4 counts the 4 levels of the perfect tree instead of its 3 edges.
Choosing 3 and 15: the minimum is right but the maximum counts the 15 nodes of the chain instead of its 14 edges.

recognize.clues: The minimum and maximum possible height are asked for a given node count, and the note says a single node has height 0. That means counting nodes per level and converting levels to edges.
recognize.contrast: Not AVL height, where the balance rule caps the height. A plain BST has no balance rule, so a chain is allowed.

check.body: Test the formulas on 3 nodes, where drawing the shapes gives a shortest height of 1 and a tallest of 2. The formulas $\lceil \log_2 (n+1) \rceil - 1$ and $n - 1$ give the same two values. For 15 nodes, a tree of height 2 holds at most 7, so no tree that short can take all 15.
